Deep beneath your feet, Earth is very hot. Most of the time, you cannot feel that heat. But in some places, it bursts out through the ground in a volcano.

Earth is made of layers. The outer layer, called the crust, is a thin shell of solid rock. It is broken into giant pieces called plates, which fit together like a puzzle. Under the crust is the mantle. In some places, rock deep in the mantle melts. This melted rock is called magma.

Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises. It collects in a pool called a magma chamber, a few miles below the surface. Gas bubbles in the magma build up pressure, much like the bubbles in a shaken bottle of soda. When the pressure becomes too great, the magma pushes up through cracks in the crust and bursts out. This is called an eruption. Once magma reaches the surface, it has a new name: lava.

Not all eruptions are the same. Some volcanoes, like the ones in Hawaii, have runny lava that flows gently out of the ground. People can sometimes stand at a safe distance and watch glowing rivers of lava move downhill. Other volcanoes have thick, sticky magma that traps gas. When these volcanoes erupt, they explode violently. They can blast ash and rock miles into the sky. In 1980, Mount St. Helens in Washington State erupted this way. The blast knocked down forests for miles around.

Over time, layers of cooled lava and ash pile up around the opening. Layer by layer, they build a mountain. Some volcanoes grow very tall. Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises more than 33,000 feet from the ocean floor. Measured from its base, it is taller than Mount Everest.

Volcanoes can be dangerous, but they also help people. Volcanic ash breaks down into rich soil that is good for growing crops. Many islands, including all of the Hawaiian Islands, were formed by volcanoes.

Scientists who study volcanoes are called volcanologists. They use special tools to measure small earthquakes, changes in the shape of the ground, and gases coming from a volcano. These signs can warn that an eruption may be coming soon. With enough warning, people who live nearby can move to safety.
Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?

["All volcanoes explode and blast ash into the sky.","Volcanologists are scientists who study earthquakes.","Volcanoes form when magma rises and erupts, and they can both harm and help people.","Mount St. Helens is the most dangerous volcano in the world."]
The passage explains how volcanoes form and erupt, then tells how they can be dangerous but also create soil and islands.

Deep beneath your feet, Earth is very hot. Most of the time, you cannot feel that heat. But in some places, it bursts out through the ground in a volcano.

Earth is made of layers. The outer layer, called the crust, is a thin shell of solid rock. It is broken into giant pieces called plates, which fit together like a puzzle. Under the crust is the mantle. In some places, rock deep in the mantle melts. This melted rock is called magma.

Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises. It collects in a pool called a magma chamber, a few miles below the surface. Gas bubbles in the magma build up pressure, much like the bubbles in a shaken bottle of soda. When the pressure becomes too great, the magma pushes up through cracks in the crust and bursts out. This is called an eruption. Once magma reaches the surface, it has a new name: lava.

Not all eruptions are the same. Some volcanoes, like the ones in Hawaii, have runny lava that flows gently out of the ground. People can sometimes stand at a safe distance and watch glowing rivers of lava move downhill. Other volcanoes have thick, sticky magma that traps gas. When these volcanoes erupt, they explode violently. They can blast ash and rock miles into the sky. In 1980, Mount St. Helens in Washington State erupted this way. The blast knocked down forests for miles around.

The children laughed loudly at the silly clown.
"Loudly" tells how the children laughed, so it is an adverb. "Silly" is an adjective that describes the clown.

["Where did you put my library book","I put the book on the shelf","Please put my book on the shelf","What a great book this is"]
"Where did you put my library book" asks a question, so it needs a question mark. The others are a command, a statement, and an exclamation.

Leo did not want to spend his summer vacation pulling weeds. His mother had signed him up to volunteer at the community garden on Maple Street, and he was not happy about it. "All of my friends are swimming at the neighborhood pool," he grumbled as they walked down the sunny block together.

At the garden, an elderly woman named Mrs. Alvarez waved them over. She wore a wide straw hat, and there was dirt on both of her knees. "You must be Leo," she said with a friendly smile. "I have been waiting all week for a strong helper, and this little plot belongs to you now."

Leo stared at a small square of dry, lumpy soil that did not look like much at all. Mrs. Alvarez handed him a packet of tomato seeds and a tiny shovel. She demonstrated how to dig shallow holes, drop in the seeds, and pat the dirt down gently with his palm. "Water them every single morning," she instructed. "Plants are patient, but they are never forgetful."

For two long weeks, absolutely nothing happened. Leo watered the bare soil each day and felt ridiculous. Then one morning, he noticed tiny green sprouts poking up through the dirt. He knelt down carefully and counted twelve of them! He raced across the garden to tell Mrs. Alvarez, and she laughed and clapped her hands.

By the middle of July, the tomato plants were taller than his waist. However, one morning Leo discovered that something had chewed the leaves and nibbled two green tomatoes. He also noticed small paw prints in the mud. "Rabbits," Mrs. Alvarez said, shaking her head. Leo felt his face get hot, because all of his hard work seemed ruined.

That afternoon, Leo did not hurry home early. Instead, he located some old wire and wooden stakes behind the tool shed. He spent three hours constructing a low fence around his plot. His fingers got scratched, but he refused to stop until every gap was closed.

The fence worked perfectly. In August, Leo picked his first ripe tomato, which was warm from the sun and bright red. He carried a heavy basket to Mrs. Alvarez and offered her the biggest one.

"Next summer," Leo announced, "may I grow peppers too?"
Which sentence best states a theme of the story?

["Older people always know more than young people.","Wild animals should never be allowed near a garden.","It is better to spend the summer with friends at the pool.","Patience and hard work can turn something small into something rewarding."]
Leo waits two weeks for sprouts, fixes the rabbit problem by building a fence, and is finally rewarded with ripe tomatoes. The story shows that patience and hard work pay off.

Long ago in ancient Greece, a young woman named Arachne lived in a small village near the sea. Her family was poor, but Arachne had a special talent. She could weave cloth more beautifully than anyone in the land. Her pictures in thread showed rivers that seemed to ripple and birds that looked ready to fly away.

People came from faraway towns just to watch her work. "Surely the goddess Athena taught you this skill," they often said. Athena was the goddess of wisdom and weaving. The people of the village believed every great weaver owed her thanks.

Arachne would toss her head proudly. "Nobody taught me anything," she boasted. "My skill belongs to me alone. In fact, I am a better weaver than Athena herself. If she disagrees, let her come and try to beat me."

High on Mount Olympus, Athena heard these arrogant words. She dressed herself as a bent old woman and walked into the village. She gently warned Arachne, "Be careful, child. Ask the goddess to forgive you before it is too late." Arachne only laughed at the stranger and said her challenge again.

Suddenly the old woman vanished, and Athena stood there, tall and shining. The people dropped to their knees, but Arachne did not say she was sorry. Instead, she set up her loom, and the contest began.

Athena wove a grand scene of the gods sitting on their thrones. Arachne wove a picture that made fun of the gods and showed their mistakes. Her threads were so fine and her colors so bright that even Athena could not find a single flaw. Still, the goddess was furious that a human would mock the gods so boldly.

Athena touched Arachne lightly on the forehead. At once, Arachne began to shrink. Her arms and legs grew thin, and soon she had eight of them. Her body became small and round. Arachne had been changed into the very first spider.

"You love to weave," Athena said, "so you and your children will weave forever." From that day on, Arachne spun thin, silky webs in the corners of houses and between the branches of trees.

The people of ancient Greece told this story to remind others that talent is a gift. Even the most skillful person should stay humble.
What lesson does this myth teach?
["Spiders are helpful animals that should be protected.","Strangers should never be trusted.","People should practice every day to improve a skill.","Even very talented people should stay humble."]
The last paragraph says the story reminds people that talent is a gift and that even the most skillful person should stay humble.

In the spring of 1848, eleven-year-old Hannah Brooks left her home in Missouri. Her family had sold their farm, packed everything into a covered wagon, and joined a wagon train heading west on the Oregon Trail. Her father dreamed of rich farmland in Oregon, more than two thousand miles away.

The journey was harder than Hannah had imagined. Each day, the wagons rolled slowly across the endless prairie. Hannah walked beside the wagon for hours because the oxen were already pulling a heavy load. At night, she gathered dried buffalo chips for the cooking fire, since there were almost no trees to burn.

After six weeks, the wagon train reached a wide, muddy river. The water was brown and fast after the spring rains. The wagon master studied the river for a long time. "We cannot wait for the water to go down," he announced. "Snow will close the mountain passes if we arrive too late."

Hannah's little brother, Thomas, grabbed her hand. He was only six, and his lip was trembling. "What if the wagon tips over?" he whispered. Hannah was frightened too, and her stomach felt tight. However, she did not want Thomas to see her fear.

"Papa has crossed rivers before," she told him calmly. "We will hold on tight and sing our counting song. By the time we reach one hundred, we will be on the other side."

The men raised the wagon boxes onto blocks of wood so the water would not soak their supplies. Then Papa cracked the whip, and the oxen stepped into the cold current. The wagon rocked and creaked. Water splashed over the sides, and a sack of flour floated away. Hannah held Thomas tightly and kept counting out loud, even when her voice shook.

At last, the oxen climbed onto the far bank. The family was soaked, and they had lost some flour, but everyone was safe. Mama hugged both children and looked at Hannah with surprise. "You were so brave," she said softly.

That night, Hannah wrote in her small journal by the light of the campfire. "Today I learned that being brave does not mean you are not scared," she wrote. "It means you keep going anyway."
Why does the wagon master decide NOT to wait for the river to go down?
["Snow could close the mountain passes if they arrive too late.","Another wagon train is waiting behind them.","The families have run out of flour.","The oxen are too tired to keep walking."]
The wagon master says, "Snow will close the mountain passes if we arrive too late." That is the cause of his decision.

When you flip a light switch, the room fills with light right away. It may seem like magic, but it is really science. The light turns on because electricity is moving along a path called a circuit.

Electricity is a form of energy. It is made of tiny bits called electrons that move from place to place. But electrons cannot move just anywhere. They need a complete path that forms a loop. That loop is a circuit.

A simple circuit has three main parts. First, it needs a source of energy, such as a battery. Second, it needs wires to carry the current. Third, it needs something that uses the energy, like a light bulb or a small motor. All of these parts must be joined in an unbroken loop. Then electrons can flow from the battery, through the wire and the bulb, and back to the battery again.

There are two kinds of circuits you should know about. In a closed circuit, the path is complete. The current can flow, so the bulb glows. In an open circuit, there is a gap somewhere in the path. Because the loop is broken, the electrons stop moving and the bulb goes dark. A switch is just a tool that opens and closes a circuit. When you turn a switch off, you make a gap on purpose.

Not every material lets current pass through it easily. Materials that let it flow are called conductors. Most metals, such as copper and steel, are good conductors. That is why the wires inside your walls are usually made of copper. Materials that block the flow are called insulators. Rubber, plastic, glass, and wood are common insulators. Power cords are covered with plastic or rubber. This coat keeps the current inside the wire, so it does not shock the person who is holding the cord.

Knowing about circuits helps people stay safe. Water from a river or a sink can carry current, so you should never touch a switch or plug with wet hands. You should also never poke anything into an outlet. Electricity is useful, but it can be dangerous when it goes where it should not go.

The next time you turn on a lamp, think about the hidden loop that makes it work.
What is the main idea of the passage?

["Batteries are the only source of energy for light bulbs.","Copper is the most useful metal in the world.","Light switches were invented to save energy in homes.","Electricity flows through a complete loop called a circuit, and knowing how circuits work helps people stay safe."]
The whole passage explains what a circuit is, its parts, open and closed circuits, conductors and insulators, and safety.

When you flip a light switch, the room fills with light right away. It may seem like magic, but it is really science. The light turns on because electricity is moving along a path called a circuit.

Electricity is a form of energy. It is made of tiny bits called electrons that move from place to place. But electrons cannot move just anywhere. They need a complete path that forms a loop. That loop is a circuit.

A simple circuit has three main parts. First, it needs a source of energy, such as a battery. Second, it needs wires to carry the current. Third, it needs something that uses the energy, like a light bulb or a small motor. All of these parts must be joined in an unbroken loop. Then electrons can flow from the battery, through the wire and the bulb, and back to the battery again.

There are two kinds of circuits you should know about. In a closed circuit, the path is complete. The current can flow, so the bulb glows. In an open circuit, there is a gap somewhere in the path. Because the loop is broken, the electrons stop moving and the bulb goes dark. A switch is just a tool that opens and closes a circuit. When you turn a switch off, you make a gap on purpose.

Two hundred years ago, moving goods across New York State was slow and costly. Farmers in the West grew plenty of wheat and corn, but getting their crops to cities on the East Coast was a big problem. Roads were rough and muddy. Wagons pulled by horses could carry only small loads, and a trip could take weeks.

DeWitt Clinton, who later became governor of New York, had a bold idea. He wanted to dig a canal, or a man-made river, across the state. It would connect the Hudson River near Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo. Boats could then travel all the way from the Great Lakes to New York City by water.

Many people laughed at the plan. The canal would need to stretch about 363 miles through forests, swamps, and hills. Some people called it "Clinton's Ditch" and said it would never work. Still, Clinton did not give up, and digging began on July 4, 1817.

Building the canal was very hard work. Thousands of workers used shovels, picks, and horses to dig the long ditch. Many of the workers were new arrivals from Ireland. They cleared trees, pulled out stumps, and moved tons of dirt and rock. In some places, the land rose or fell too steeply for boats. To solve this problem, workers built locks. A lock is like a water elevator that raises or lowers a boat from one level to the next.

In 1825, after eight years of work, the Erie Canal was finally finished. Boats were pulled along the water by mules that walked on a path beside the canal. The trip that once took weeks by wagon now took about ten days. The cost of shipping goods dropped to about one tenth of what it had been.

The canal changed the country in many ways. Towns such as Syracuse, Rochester, and Buffalo grew quickly along its banks. New York City became the busiest port in the United States. Settlers also used the canal to travel west, which helped new states grow.

Today, trains and trucks carry most goods. However, people still ride boats on parts of the Erie Canal for fun and remember the "ditch" that changed America.

Garrett Morgan was born in 1877 in Paris, Kentucky. His parents had once been enslaved, and his family worked hard to make a living. Garrett went to school only until about the sixth grade. But he never stopped learning. He loved to find out how machines worked. He would take them apart and put them back together.

As a teenager, Garrett moved north to Ohio to look for work. He settled in the city of Cleveland and got a job fixing sewing machines. He became so skilled that he soon opened his own repair shop. Later, he started other businesses as well, such as a shop that made clothing.

Garrett was always looking for ways to solve problems. He noticed that firefighters often got sick from breathing thick smoke. So he designed a safety hood that covered a person's head. A long tube hung down near the floor, where the air was cleaner. With this hood, a person could breathe more safely in a room full of smoke. Garrett got a patent for his invention in 1914.

Two years later, his hood was put to a real test. In 1916, a blast trapped workers in a tunnel under Lake Erie. The tunnel filled with deadly gas, and rescuers could not get inside. Garrett and his brother rushed to the scene with his safety hoods. They went down into the tunnel. They helped carry several men out to safety. Because of their bravery, more fire departments became interested in his hood.

Garrett also cared about safety on the roads. In the early 1900s, cars, horses, bikes, and people all shared busy streets. Many early traffic signals had only two signs, "Stop" and "Go." They switched with no warning, so crashes were common. One day Garrett saw a bad crash. He decided to make a better signal. His design added a third position that stopped traffic in all directions for a moment. This gave drivers time to slow down before the signal changed. He got a patent for it in 1923. Later, he sold the rights to a large company.

Garrett Morgan died in 1963. Today, his ideas live on in the masks that protect rescue workers. They also live on in the traffic lights that warn drivers before they must stop at a busy corner.
What is the author's main purpose in writing this passage?
["to tell about an inventor whose ideas helped keep people safe","to persuade readers to become firefighters","to describe what life was like in Kentucky","to explain how to repair a sewing machine"]

Choose the verb that best completes the sentence.

At this time tomorrow, I ___ on an airplane to Seoul.

Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

It is a school rule: you ___ wear a helmet when you ride your bike to school.
"It is a school rule" shows that wearing a helmet is required, so the modal "must" is correct.

Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Take your umbrella. It ___ rain later, but I am not sure.
"I am not sure" shows that rain is only possible, so use "might."

Choose the words in the correct order.

We adopted a ___ puppy.
["white little cute","little cute white","cute little white","cute white little"]
Adjectives usually go in this order: opinion (cute), size (little), color (white).

Choose the words in the correct order.

My grandmother has a ___ table in her kitchen.
["beautiful old wooden","beautiful wooden old","wooden old beautiful","old wooden beautiful"]
The order is opinion (beautiful), age (old), material (wooden).

Choose the words in the correct order.

Dad bought me a ___ sweater for the winter.

The order is age (new), color (red), material (wool).

Which group of words is the prepositional phrase in this sentence?

The cat slept under the warm blanket.
["The cat","slept under","The cat slept","under the warm blanket"]
A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition (under) and ends with a noun (blanket): "under the warm blanket."
Which of these is a complete sentence?
["After the movie ended.","Running down the long hallway.","The bus was late this morning.","Because the bus was late."]
"The bus was late this morning" has a subject (the bus) and a verb (was) and expresses a complete thought. The others are fragments.
Which of these is a run-on sentence?
["The sun came out. We went to the beach.","When the sun came out, we went to the beach.","The sun came out we went to the beach.","The sun came out, so we went to the beach."]
"The sun came out we went to the beach" joins two complete sentences with no punctuation or conjunction, so it is a run-on.

I was hungry I ate a sandwich.
["I was hungry so, I ate a sandwich.","I was hungry, so I ate a sandwich.","I was hungry I ate, a sandwich.","I was, hungry I ate a sandwich."]
Add a comma and the conjunction "so" between the two complete thoughts.

The first word, the month (July), the place name (Grand Canyon), and the state (Arizona) are capitalized. "Family" is a common noun.

Lily studied hard for the test and she got every answer right.

Every Saturday morning, Tomás rode his bicycle to the Oak Hill Animal Shelter, where he walked the dogs and scrubbed the food bowls. Most of the dogs leaped against their gates whenever he passed, barking and wagging as if he were a celebrity. One dog, however, never moved at all. She was a thin brown mutt named Pepper, and she spent every day pressed into the farthest corner of her kennel.

"Pepper was discovered living under a bridge," explained Ms. Okafor, the shelter director. "Nobody knows what happened to her before that, and she doesn't trust people yet."

Tomás tried every idea he could imagine. He called her name in a cheerful voice, offered treats through the bars, and even squeaked a rubber chicken. Each time, Pepper only trembled and turned her face toward the wall.

After three discouraging weeks, Tomás was ready to quit. "She just doesn't like me," he told Ms. Okafor.

Ms. Okafor smiled patiently. "Maybe you're trying too hard. Imagine a stranger running toward you and shouting your name. Would that make you feel safe?"

Tomás remembered his first day at his new school last fall. Everyone had crowded around him with questions, and all he had wanted to do was disappear.

The following Saturday, Tomás tried a different approach. He brought a library book, sat on the floor outside Pepper's kennel, and read aloud in a low, quiet voice. He did not look at her, and he did not offer any treats; he simply read.

For the first hour, nothing happened, and the next Saturday was the same. On the third Saturday, however, Tomás heard a soft scraping sound. From the corner of his eye, he noticed Pepper creep a few inches closer before she lay down with her nose resting against the bars.

Tomás continued reading, but his heart was pounding like a drum.

By the end of the month, Pepper was waiting at the front of her kennel whenever Tomás arrived, and her tail swept back and forth across the floor. When he finally opened the gate, she climbed into his lap as if she had always belonged there.

Ms. Okafor shook her head in amazement and asked how he had done it.

Tomás scratched Pepper behind the ears. "I stopped asking her to trust me," he said, "and just gave her time."
Which sentence best states the theme of the story?

["People should give up on a goal after a few weeks of trying.","Trust often grows slowly when someone is patient and gentle.","Reading out loud is the best way to train any animal.","Shelter dogs are happiest when people give them lots of treats."]

Pepper begins to trust Tomás only after he stops pushing and quietly gives her time, as his last line says. The other choices are not supported; treats and squeaky toys did not work, and Tomás succeeds because he does not give up.

Anika had been a reporter for the Lincoln Ledger, her school's newspaper, for only a month when she stumbled onto the biggest news of the year. She was waiting in the cafeteria line when she overheard Mr. Haddad, the head cook, talking to a helper.

"After this week, we're finished with the Friday pizza," he said.

Anika nearly dropped her tray, because Pizza Friday was the most popular day at Lincoln Elementary. That afternoon she wrote an article with the headline "No More Pizza Fridays!" The editor, a sixth grader named Marcus, loved it, and the story appeared on the front page the next morning.

By lunchtime, the whole school was in an uproar. Fourth graders made protest signs, and a group of fifth graders started a petition that collected two hundred names. Anika felt proud, since her first big story had everyone talking.

Then Mr. Haddad stopped her in the hallway, looking puzzled rather than angry.

"Anika, I read your article," he said. "We aren't getting rid of pizza. We're getting rid of the frozen pizza, and starting next month, my team is going to make it fresh with homemade dough and real vegetables."

Anika's face grew hot with embarrassment. She had heard only half of the conversation, and she had never asked Mr. Haddad a single question.

She hurried to the newspaper office to find Marcus and announced that they needed to fix the mistake.

Marcus shrugged. "Everyone will forget about it in a week. If we print a correction, people will decide the Ledger can't be trusted."

Anika thought about the petition, the signs, and the younger students who were truly upset. "If we don't fix it," she said slowly, "then they really shouldn't trust us."

That evening she wrote a new article. This time she interviewed Mr. Haddad for twenty minutes, asking about the new recipe, the cost, and when the change would begin. At the top of the page, she added a note: "Last week the Ledger reported that pizza was being removed from the menu, which was wrong, and I am sorry."

The next Friday, students lined up early for the first homemade pizza. While Anika waited, a fourth grader tapped her on the shoulder and asked whether she was the reporter who had written the correction.

When Anika nodded, the girl grinned. "I'm going to read everything you write from now on."
What is the main problem in the story?

["Marcus refuses to let Anika write for the school newspaper.","The fifth graders cannot collect enough names for their petition.","Mr. Haddad decides to stop serving pizza at Lincoln Elementary.","Anika publishes a story that is wrong because she did not check her facts."]
Anika writes "No More Pizza Fridays!" after hearing only half of a conversation, and the whole story is about how she deals with that mistake. Mr. Haddad never planned to stop serving pizza.

Long ago, in a green valley between two mountains, an elderly farmer named Bao divided his land between his two sons. To Kiet, the elder, he gave the eastern field, and to Lan, the younger, he gave the western field. "Use the soil wisely," Bao told them, "and it will feed you for the rest of your lives."

Kiet wasted no time. That very spring he planted melons, which grew quickly and sold for a handsome price at the market. By autumn his pockets jingled with coins, and he purchased an elegant new coat.

Lan did something that puzzled everyone in the village. He planted rows of tiny walnut trees that were no taller than his knee. Because walnut trees require many years to produce nuts, Lan had nothing to sell for a long time. He earned a little money by repairing fences for his neighbors, and he wore the same patched shirt year after year.

Kiet scoffed at his younger brother. "You are planting for an old man, but I am planting for today."

Lan only smiled and continued watering his saplings.

Eight summers passed, and then came a terrible year when no rain fell at all. The river shrank to a muddy trickle, and the sun baked the valley floor until it cracked. Kiet's melons withered on their vines before they could ripen. He planted a second crop, but it died as well, and by winter his coins had disappeared and his elegant coat had worn thin.

On the western side of the valley, however, the walnut trees stood tall and healthy. Over the years their roots had grown deep enough to reach water far beneath the dry ground. That autumn the branches sagged with nuts, and Lan filled sack after sack.

One frosty evening Kiet knocked on his brother's door. He stared at his boots and could not find any words to say.

Lan placed a heavy sack in his brother's arms. "Father gave us two fields," he said, "but he raised us as one family."

The next spring, the brothers worked side by side. In the eastern field they planted melons to sell that summer, and along its edges they planted walnut trees for the years to come. Kiet dug every hole himself, and this time he did not complain about waiting.

["It is always better to grow fruit than to grow trees.","Planning for the future can be wiser than seeking quick rewards.","Hard work never matters when the weather is bad.","Older brothers should make all the decisions for a family."]
Kiet's quick melon profits disappear in the drought, while Lan's slow-growing walnut trees survive and feed both brothers. In the end even Kiet plants trees "for the years to come."

Make a fist and squeeze it as hard as you can. Now open and squeeze it again, about once every second. Your hand will probably grow tired within a few minutes. Yet a muscle about the size of that fist has been squeezing inside your chest every second of your life, and it never takes a break. That muscle is your heart.

The heart is the center of the circulatory system, the body system that moves blood to every part of you. Blood carries oxygen from the air you breathe and nutrients from the food you eat. Every cell in your body needs these supplies to stay alive and do its job. Blood also carries away wastes, such as carbon dioxide, that cells must get rid of.

Blood travels through tubes called blood vessels. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins carry blood back to it. Between them are capillaries, tiny vessels thinner than a hair. In the capillaries, oxygen and nutrients pass out of the blood and into the cells, and wastes pass in. If you could lay all of your blood vessels end to end, they would stretch around Earth more than twice.

The heart itself has four rooms, or chambers, and the two on the right side pump blood to the lungs. There the blood drops off carbon dioxide, which you breathe out, and picks up fresh oxygen. The blood then returns to the left side of the heart. The left side pumps this oxygen-rich blood out to the rest of the body. Because the left side has the harder job, its walls are thicker and stronger.

Each time the heart squeezes, it pushes a wave of blood through the arteries. You can feel this wave, called your pulse, in your wrist or neck. When you run or jump, your muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster to deliver it.

Like any muscle, the heart grows stronger with exercise. Playing outside, riding a bike, and dancing all give your heart a workout. Eating nutritious foods and getting enough sleep help, too. Take care of your heart, and it will keep working hard for you.

["The left side of the heart is stronger than the right side.","The heart pumps blood through blood vessels to deliver what the body needs and remove wastes.","Exercise is the only way to keep the body healthy.","Blood vessels are long enough to stretch around Earth."]
Most of the passage explains how the heart and blood vessels move blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to cells and takes wastes away. The other choices are smaller details.

The Grand Canyon in Arizona is more than a mile deep in some places. Standing at its edge, you might guess that a giant once carved it with a shovel. The real sculptors were much smaller and much slower: water, wind, and ice working for millions of years.

Scientists use two words to describe how the land changes. Weathering is the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces. Erosion is the moving of those pieces from one place to another. Weathering makes the pieces, and erosion carries them away.

Weathering happens in several ways. In cold places, rain seeps into small cracks in rock. When the temperature drops, the water freezes and expands, pushing the crack a little wider. After the ice melts, more water flows in. Over many winters, this cycle can split a boulder in two. Plants cause weathering, too. A tree root growing into a crack acts like a slowly opening wedge. Even the acid in rainwater can dissolve some kinds of rock, such as limestone.

Once rock has been broken apart, erosion goes to work. Moving water is the most powerful force of erosion on Earth. Rivers pick up sand and pebbles and tumble them downstream, scraping the riverbed as they go. That is exactly how the Colorado River cut the Grand Canyon, grinding a little deeper year after year. Wind can also cause erosion, especially in deserts, where it blasts sand against rocks. In very cold regions, enormous sheets of ice called glaciers creep downhill and drag huge rocks along with them.

The pieces that erosion carries away do not vanish. Eventually, the water or wind slows down and drops them. This process is called deposition. A river that empties into the sea may leave behind so much mud and sand that it builds new land. The area of land that forms at the mouth of a river is called a delta.

Weathering and erosion can cause problems for people. They can wash away farm soil and weaken roads and bridges. Farmers plant grass and trees to hold the soil in place, and towns build walls to protect their beaches. Still, these forces never stop, slowly reshaping the land beneath our feet.
What is the difference between weathering and erosion?

["Weathering breaks rock into pieces, and erosion moves the pieces away.","Weathering happens only in deserts, and erosion happens only in rivers.","Weathering is caused by people, and erosion is caused by nature.","Weathering builds new land, and erosion destroys it."]
The passage says, "Weathering makes the pieces, and erosion carries them away." The other choices are not stated and are not true.

After the ice melts, more water flows in. Over many winters, this cycle can split a boulder in two. Plants cause weathering, too. A tree root growing into a crack acts like a slowly opening wedge. Even the acid in rainwater can dissolve some kinds of rock, such as limestone.

Once rock has been broken apart, erosion goes to work. Moving water is the most powerful force of erosion on Earth. Rivers pick up sand and pebbles and tumble them downstream, scraping the riverbed as they go. That is exactly how the Colorado River cut the Grand Canyon, grinding a little deeper year after year. Wind can also cause erosion, especially in deserts, where it blasts sand against rocks. In very cold regions, enormous sheets of ice called glaciers creep downhill and drag huge rocks along with them.

The pieces that erosion carries away do not vanish. Eventually, the water or wind slows down and drops them. This process is called deposition. A river that empties into the sea may leave behind so much mud and sand that it builds new land. The area of land that forms at the mouth of a river is called a delta.

Weathering and erosion can cause problems for people. They can wash away farm soil and weaken roads and bridges. Farmers plant grass and trees to hold the soil in place, and towns build walls to protect their beaches. Still, these forces never stop, slowly reshaping the land beneath our feet.
Why does the author compare a tree root to "a slowly opening wedge"?
["to prove that plants grow faster than rocks","to help readers picture how a root pushes rock apart as it grows","to show that tree roots are made of metal","to explain how farmers cut down trees"]
A wedge is a tool that is forced into a gap to split something. The comparison helps readers imagine a growing root slowly forcing a crack in a rock to widen.

Imagine a classroom where one student made all the rules, decided who broke them, and chose every punishment. That student would have a lot of power, and the others would have very little say. The people who wrote the United States Constitution in 1787 worried about this kind of problem. They had just fought a war to escape the rule of a king, and they did not want any one person or group to become too powerful.

Their solution was to divide the national government into three parts, called branches. Each branch has its own job.

The legislative branch makes the laws. It is called Congress, and it has two parts, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Members of Congress are elected by the people of each state. When they want to create a new law, they write a plan called a bill. Both parts of Congress must vote to approve it.

The executive branch carries out the laws. The president leads this branch. After Congress passes a bill, the president can sign it into law. The president also commands the military and works with leaders of other countries. Many departments help the president, such as the ones that work on schools, farms, and national parks.

The judicial branch explains the laws. It includes the Supreme Court and many lower courts. Judges decide what laws mean and whether they follow the rules in the Constitution. If the Supreme Court decides that a law breaks those rules, the law can no longer be used.

The writers of the Constitution also gave each branch ways to limit the others. This idea is called checks and balances. For example, the president can veto, or reject, a bill that Congress has passed. However, Congress can still turn that bill into a law if two-thirds of the members in each part of Congress vote for it again. The president chooses judges for the Supreme Court, but the Senate must agree to each choice.

Checks and balances can make the government move slowly, because the branches often have to work together and compromise. Yet that is exactly what the writers wanted. By sharing power, the three branches help protect the rights of every citizen.
Why did the writers of the Constitution divide the government into three branches?

["They needed more jobs for people who had fought in the war.","They did not want any one person or group to become too powerful.","They wanted the government to make decisions as quickly as possible.","They wanted the president to make all of the laws."]

The words ERUPT, INTERRUPT, and RUPTURE all share the Latin root RUPT. What does RUPT most likely mean?
A volcano erupts when it breaks open, and you interrupt when you break into a conversation, so RUPT means "break."
MANUAL, MANUSCRIPT, and MANUFACTURE all contain the Latin root MANU. What does MANU most likely mean?
A manual task is done by hand, and a manuscript was once written by hand, so MANU means "hand."
PEDAL, PEDESTRIAN, and CENTIPEDE all contain the Latin root PED. What does PED mean?
You push a pedal with your foot, a pedestrian travels on foot, and a centipede seems to have a hundred feet, so PED means "foot."
What does the prefix SEMI- mean in the word SEMICIRCLE?
A semicircle is half of a circle. SEMI- means "half" or "partly," as in semifinal.
What does the suffix -IST mean in the words ARTIST and SCIENTIST?
["the state of being","a person who does or studies something","full of","in the direction of"]
An artist is a person who makes art, and a scientist is a person who studies science, so -IST means "a person who does or studies something."
What does the suffix -WARD mean in the words HOMEWARD and UPWARD?
["without","one who","able to be","in the direction of"]
Homeward means "toward home," and upward means "toward a higher place," so -WARD means "in the direction of."
What does the prefix NON- mean in the word NONFICTION?
Nonfiction is writing that is not made up. The prefix NON- means "not," as in nonstop and nonsense.
Which word is a SYNONYM for VERTICAL?
Something vertical goes straight up and down, so UPRIGHT is a synonym. FLAT is closer to horizontal, its opposite.
Which word is a SYNONYM for SWIFT?
SWIFT means moving with great speed, so QUICK is a synonym.
Which word is an ANTONYM for SHRINK?
To shrink is to become smaller, and to grow is to become larger. DWINDLE is a synonym for SHRINK.
Which word is an ANTONYM for ARTIFICIAL?
Something artificial is made by people, while something natural comes from nature. FAKE is close in meaning to ARTIFICIAL.
Read the sentence: "After the storm passed, the floodwater began to RECEDE, and the streets slowly dried out." What does RECEDE mean?
["move back or go down","freeze solid","rise higher","turn muddy"]
The streets "slowly dried out," which tells you the water was going away. RECEDE means to move back or become lower.
Read the sentence: "Grandma is very FRUGAL; she reuses gift wrap and never buys anything she does not need." What does FRUGAL mean?
["careful about spending money","forgetful about details","very generous with gifts","fond of shopping"]
Reusing gift wrap and buying only what she needs are clues that FRUGAL means careful not to waste money.
Read the sentence: "A fallen tree was an OBSTACLE on the trail, so the hikers had to climb over it." What is an OBSTACLE?
["a shortcut through the woods","a sign that gives directions","something that blocks the way","a place to rest"]
The hikers had to climb over the tree to keep going, so an OBSTACLE is something that blocks your way.
Read the sentence: "The twins' handwriting is nearly IDENTICAL, so even their teacher cannot tell whose paper is whose." What does IDENTICAL mean?
The teacher cannot tell the papers apart, which shows that IDENTICAL means exactly the same.
Read the sentence: "The little stream MEANDERED through the meadow, curving back and forth like a ribbon." What does MEANDERED mean?
["rushed straight ahead","followed a winding path","froze over","dried up completely"]
The clue "curving back and forth like a ribbon" shows that MEANDERED means followed a slow, winding path.
In which sentence does FAIR mean "treating everyone equally"?
["Tomorrow the weather will be FAIR and sunny.","We rode the Ferris wheel at the county FAIR.","The referee made a FAIR call, so neither team complained.","The baby has FAIR hair and blue eyes."]
A fair call by a referee treats both teams the same way. In the other sentences FAIR means an outdoor festival, light in color, and clear weather.
In which sentence does BARK mean "the outer covering of a tree"?
["The seals BARK as they swim near the dock.","The rough BARK of the oak scraped my hands.","Our puppy will BARK at the mail carrier.","I heard a loud BARK from the yard next door."]
Only in the first sentence is BARK something on a tree that can scrape your hands. In the others it is the sound an animal makes.
Read the sentence: "The hikers filled their bottles with cold, clear water from a SPRING beside the trail." What does SPRING mean in this sentence?
["a coil of metal that bounces back","a sudden jump forward","a place where water flows up from the ground","the season after winter"]
The hikers get water from it beside the trail, so SPRING here means a natural source of water coming out of the ground.
Read the sentence: "Before dinner, Dad asked me to SET the table." What does SET mean in this sentence?
["become firm or hard","go down below the horizon","a group of things that belong together","arrange plates and silverware on"]
When you set the table, you arrange plates, cups, and silverware on it for a meal. The other choices are different meanings of SET.
Kendra joined the soccer team, the school play, and the chess club in the same week, and now she has no free time. Her dad says she BIT OFF MORE THAN SHE COULD CHEW. What does this mean?
["She refused to try anything new.","She took on more than she could handle.","She ate too much food at lunch.","She spoke without thinking first."]
Joining three activities at once left Kendra with no free time. The idiom means taking on more work or responsibility than you can manage.
Marco promised to keep the surprise party a secret, but he SPILLED THE BEANS at breakfast. What does SPILLED THE BEANS mean?
["forgot about the party","made a mess at the table","cooked a big meal","told the secret too early"]
Marco was supposed to keep a secret, so SPILLED THE BEANS means he revealed it before he should have.
When Ruby said the story was really about friendship, the teacher smiled and said, "You HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD." What did the teacher mean?
["Ruby needed to try again.","Ruby had hurt her hand.","Ruby was speaking too loudly.","Ruby was exactly right."]
The teacher smiles because Ruby found the true theme. HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD means to say something exactly right.
My cousins live far away, so we see them only ONCE IN A BLUE MOON. What does ONCE IN A BLUE MOON mean?
["every night","during the winter","in the evening","very rarely"]
Because the cousins live far away, the family seldom sees them. ONCE IN A BLUE MOON means very rarely.
What does the saying DON'T JUDGE A BOOK BY ITS COVER mean?

["Take good care of library books so the covers stay clean.","Don't decide what someone or something is like based only on how it looks.","Books with plain covers are usually the most interesting.","Always read the whole book before you write a report."]
The saying warns that outward appearance does not always show what is inside or what a person is really like.
What does the saying TWO HEADS ARE BETTER THAN ONE mean?

["It is better to have two teachers in every classroom.","People should always work alone to avoid arguments.","Two people working together can often solve a problem better than one person alone.","Thinking about a problem twice is a waste of time."]
The saying means that sharing ideas with another person often leads to a better solution.
Complete the analogy. STETHOSCOPE is to DOCTOR as HAMMER is to ______.
A stethoscope is a tool a doctor uses, and a hammer is a tool a carpenter uses. The relationship is tool to worker.
Complete the analogy. FOAL is to HORSE as CUB is to ______.
A foal is a young horse, and a cub is a young bear. The relationship is young animal to adult animal.
Which word shows the STRONGEST degree of happiness?
All four words describe happiness, but OVERJOYED means extremely happy, while CONTENT, PLEASED, and GLAD are milder.
Your teacher asks you to PARAPHRASE a paragraph from your science book. What should you do?
["copy it word for word","read it aloud to a partner","restate its ideas in your own words","draw a diagram of it"]
To PARAPHRASE means to explain the same ideas using your own words instead of the author's exact words.

Choose the relative pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"The lifeguard ______ pulled the swimmer from the waves received an award."
WHO refers to a person and is the subject of the clause; the lifeguard is the one who pulled the swimmer.

Choose the relative pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"The library book ______ I borrowed last month is overdue."
THAT refers to things, such as a book. WHO and WHOM refer to people, and WHOSE shows ownership.

Choose the relative pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"Mr. Ortiz, ______ dog won first prize at the show, lives across the street."
WHOSE shows possession; the dog belongs to Mr. Ortiz.

Choose the relative pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"The new student, ______ I met at lunch, just moved here from Brazil."
The pronoun refers to a person and is the object of MET (I met her), so the object form WHOM is correct.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"By the end of this school year, I ______ fifty books."
The phrase "by the end of this school year" points to an action that will be finished before a future time, which calls for the future perfect tense.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"When the power went out, I ______ a shower."
The past progressive WAS TAKING shows an action that was in progress when another past event, the power going out, interrupted it.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Last night the wind ______ our patio chairs into the neighbor's yard."
BLOW is an irregular verb; its simple past form is BLEW. BLOWED is not a word, and BLOWN needs a helping verb.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Have you ever ______ a horse?"
After the helping verb HAVE, use the past participle. The past participle of RIDE is RIDDEN.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"The flock of geese ______ south every fall."
The subject is FLOCK, a singular collective noun, so it takes the singular verb FLIES. "Of geese" is a phrase that does not change the subject.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Mathematics ______ my favorite subject this year."
MATHEMATICS ends in -s but is a singular subject, so it takes the singular verb IS.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"There ______ three baby birds in the nest outside my window."
In a sentence that begins with THERE, the subject comes after the verb. The subject BIRDS is plural, so the verb is ARE.

Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"Ms. Lee asked Sam and ______ to carry the boxes to the gym."
The pronoun is an object of the verb ASKED, so the object pronoun ME is correct. Try it alone: "Ms. Lee asked me."

Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"The campers set up the tents by ______."
THEMSELVES is the correct reflexive pronoun for a plural subject. THEIRSELVES, THEMSELF, and THEIRSELF are not standard English.

Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"Every student must bring ______ own water bottle on the field trip."
EVERY STUDENT is singular, so in formal school English the pronoun is HIS OR HER. ITS is used for things, and OUR does not match the antecedent.

Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.
"Of all the planets in our solar system, Jupiter is the ______."
When comparing three or more things, use the superlative form. For a short adjective like LARGE, add -EST.

Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence.
"Everyone agreed that the movie was ______ than the book."
For a long adjective like EXCITING, use MORE to compare two things. Never add -ER to a word that already uses MORE.

Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.
"That was the ______ snowstorm our town has had in fifty years."
BAD is irregular: bad, worse, worst. The sentence compares this storm with all the storms in fifty years, so the superlative WORST is correct.

Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.
"The choir sang so ______ that the audience stood up and cheered."
The word describes how the choir sang, a verb, so it must be the adverb BEAUTIFULLY.

Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.
"Diego studied hard, and he did ______ on his science test."
WELL is an adverb that describes how Diego did. GOOD is an adjective and should not describe a verb.
Which group of words is a complete sentence?
["Because the bus was late this morning.","The tall man with the red umbrella.","Running down the hallway after the bell.","The children laughed at the clown."]
A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb and must express a complete thought. The other choices are fragments.
Which of these is a run-on sentence?
["The rain stopped we went outside to play.","After the rain stopped, we went outside to play.","The rain stopped; we went outside to play.","The rain stopped, and we went outside to play."]
A run-on joins two complete sentences with no punctuation or conjunction. The other choices join the clauses correctly with a comma and AND, a dependent clause, or a semicolon.
Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?

["Maria loves; to swim her brother prefers to hike.","Maria loves to swim; her brother prefers to hike.","Maria loves to swim her brother; prefers to hike.","Maria; loves to swim her brother prefers to hike."]
A semicolon can join two complete sentences that are closely related. Each side of the semicolon must be a complete thought.
Which sentence correctly uses commas to set off an appositive (a phrase that renames a noun)?

["My neighbor, a retired pilot, taught me how to fold paper airplanes.","My, neighbor a retired pilot taught me how to fold paper airplanes.","My neighbor a retired pilot, taught me how to fold paper airplanes.","My neighbor, a retired pilot taught me how to fold paper airplanes."]
The phrase "a retired pilot" renames "my neighbor," so it needs a comma before it and a comma after it.
Which sentence uses commas correctly with city and state names?

["We moved from Tucson, Arizona to Portland Maine, last year.","We moved from Tucson, Arizona, to Portland, Maine, last year.","We moved from Tucson Arizona, to Portland Maine, last year.","We moved from, Tucson, Arizona to Portland, Maine last year."]
Put a comma between a city and its state, and another comma after the state when the sentence continues.

Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.
"The ______ basketball team practices in the gym on Tuesdays."
WOMEN is a plural that does not end in -s, so you add an apostrophe and -s to make it possessive: WOMEN'S.

Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.
"The cat licked ______ paw after dinner."
ITS (with no apostrophe) is a possessive pronoun. IT'S is a contraction that means "it is."

["Last thanksgiving, my family drove to the pacific ocean.","Last Thanksgiving, my family drove to the Pacific Ocean.","last Thanksgiving, my family drove to the Pacific Ocean.","Last Thanksgiving, my Family drove to the Pacific ocean."]
Holidays and the names of specific places, such as the Pacific Ocean, are proper nouns and are capitalized. The first word of a sentence is always capitalized.
Which sentence punctuates the dialogue correctly?
["Where are you going? \"asked Mom.\"","\"Where are you going\"? asked Mom.","\"Where are you going?\" asked Mom.","\"Where are you going.\" asked Mom?"]
The question mark belongs inside the closing quotation mark because it is part of what Mom says. Only the spoken words go inside the quotation marks.

Choose the conjunction that best completes the sentence.
"We cannot go camping this weekend ______ the rain stops."
UNLESS means "if not": the camping trip cannot happen if the rain does not stop. The other conjunctions do not make sense here.
Which sentence lists the adjectives in the correct order?

["She keeps her letters in an old wooden small box.","She keeps her letters in a wooden small old box.","She keeps her letters in a wooden old small box.","She keeps her letters in a small old wooden box."]
In English, adjectives usually go in this order: size, then age, then material. So the correct order is SMALL OLD WOODEN.

Rosa had wanted to paint the library mural since the first day of fifth grade, so when Ms. Patel announced that two students would design it together, Rosa raised her hand so quickly that her elbow cracked.

Her partner turned out to be Ethan Brooks, a quiet boy who decorated every scrap of paper with dragons. Rosa preferred to draw flowers, tropical birds, and the colorful outdoor market where her grandmother sold mangoes.

At their first meeting, Ethan unrolled an enormous sketch of a green dragon curling across the entire page and breathing fire over a castle. "This goes in the middle," he declared. "It's going to be incredible."

Rosa frowned. "It's a library, not a battlefield, and the kindergarteners will be terrified."

"Little kids love dragons," Ethan snapped. "Your flowers are boring."

The word stung like a bee. Rosa grabbed her pencil case and stood up, determined to march straight to Ms. Patel and ask for a new partner. Then she remembered something her grandmother always said: a closed fist cannot shake hands.

She sat back down. "Okay," she said slowly. "Tell me why the dragon matters so much to you."

Ethan looked surprised, and he picked nervously at the corner of his sketch. "My dad reads me dragon stories every night," he admitted. "They're the reason I actually enjoy reading."

Rosa considered that before she pulled out her own drawing. "My grandmother taught me to read using the signs at the market," she explained. "That's why every flower here has a word written beside it."

For a long moment, neither of them spoke. Then Ethan pointed at her page. "What if the dragon is flying over your market, and instead of fire, he's breathing out letters and words?"

Rosa felt a smile tug at her mouth. "And the words could transform into flowers when they land."

They worked through lunch for the rest of the week, with Ethan painting the shimmering scales while Rosa painted the market stalls and the swirling words. They still disagreed about colors, but now their arguments ended in laughter instead of slammed doors.

On the afternoon the mural was finished, a first grader stood in front of it for ten minutes, sounding out every word the dragon had breathed. Rosa and Ethan watched from the doorway, and neither of them said "I told you so." There was nothing left to win.
Which sentence best states a theme of the story?

["The best way to keep a friendship is to win every argument.","Younger students should always be the ones who choose the art in a library.","Listening to someone else's reasons can turn a conflict into something better for everyone.","Talented artists do their best work when they are allowed to work alone."]

Rosa almost quits, but when she asks Ethan why the dragon matters, they discover a shared love of reading and create a mural better than either plan. The story never says artists should work alone, never lets young students choose, and the ending says there was 'nothing left to win.'

Hannah Pratt was eleven years old in the spring of 1769, and she disliked the spinning wheel more than any other chore. It squeaked, the wool tangled, and her thread always came out lumpy. Her older sister, Abigail, could spin a smooth strand while humming a hymn, but Hannah could barely spin while holding her breath.

"Why can't we just buy cloth from the shop the way we used to?" Hannah grumbled one morning.

Mother set down her basket. "Because that cloth comes from England, and the British government has placed new taxes on many goods it sends to the colonies. Your father and the other men in town have promised not to purchase British goods until the taxes are removed. If we want new clothes, we must make them ourselves."

Hannah knew about the taxes, since everyone in town discussed them. Still, it seemed unfair that a king across the ocean could decide how she spent her mornings.

That afternoon, Abigail rushed in with news. "The minister's wife is organizing a spinning bee on Saturday," she announced. "Girls from all over town will spin together on the green to demonstrate that we can make our own cloth."

Hannah's stomach dropped. Spinning in front of the entire town would be far worse than spinning alone, because everyone would notice her lumpy thread.

For the next three evenings, Abigail sat beside her near the fire. She showed Hannah how to keep her foot steady on the pedal and how to let the wool slip gently through her fingers instead of squeezing it. Gradually, the lumps grew smaller and the thread grew smoother.

On Saturday, the green was crowded with wheels, and their steady whirring sounded like a hive full of bees. Hannah finally understood the name. Neighbors brought bread and cider, and an elderly farmer in a patched coat wandered from wheel to wheel, nodding with approval.

When he reached Hannah, she froze. He picked up the end of her thread and rolled it between his fingers. "Not perfect," he said, "but strong. Every strand helps, young lady."

By sunset, her arms ached, and Hannah's thread still had a few bumps. Yet when she looked across the green at the long rows of wheels, she felt something unexpected: pride. The squeaky wheel was no longer just a chore; it was her way of standing up for her community.
What is the main reason the town holds the spinning bee?

["to raise money so the town can pay the new British taxes","to choose which girl is the best spinner in town","to teach young girls how to bake bread and make cider","to show that the colonists can make their own cloth instead of buying British goods"]
Abigail says the girls 'will spin together on the green to demonstrate that we can make our own cloth.' This connects to the town's promise not to buy British goods while the taxes remain.

On Habitat Seven, the only green things for a million miles grew inside the greenhouse dome. Twelve-year-old Kai Mendoza had volunteered there every morning since his family moved to the moon, and he loved the earthy smell of damp soil, which was the only thing that reminded him of home.

So when the emergency alarm began to wail during breakfast, Kai dropped his spoon and raced down the corridor.

Inside the dome, the air felt thin and frigid. Rows of bean plants were drooping like exhausted soldiers, and a small maintenance robot named Pip rolled toward him with its blue light blinking rapidly.

"Heater failure in Section B," Pip announced. "Temperature is falling. Plants will freeze in approximately forty minutes."

"Where's Dr. Osei?" Kai asked.

"Dr. Osei is outside repairing the solar panels. She will not return for two hours."

Kai's heart pounded like a drum. He was not permitted to touch the heater, and the rule was printed in enormous red letters across the control panel: AUTHORIZED ADULTS ONLY.

He pressed the radio button. "Dr. Osei, the greenhouse heater is broken! What should I do?"

Only static answered, because the solar panels were located on the far side of the crater, out of range.

Kai studied the drooping plants. Those beans were not merely plants; they were dinner for forty people next month. He considered breaking the rule, and then he considered another possibility.

"Pip," he said, "the plants need heat, not necessarily the heater. What else in here produces heat?"

Pip's light flickered while it searched its files. "Grow lamps produce heat. Section A lamps are currently off for the night cycle."

Kai grinned, because switching on grow lamps was one of his regular daily responsibilities. Together, he and Pip dragged the tall lamp stands from Section A into Section B and switched them on, and warm orange light spilled across the leaves.

Kai watched the thermometer anxiously. For ten long minutes, the number barely moved, but then it crept upward one degree, then two.

When Dr. Osei finally hurried through the airlock, she discovered Kai asleep against a lamp stand, with Pip parked beside him like a loyal dog. Every bean plant was standing tall.

She read the computer log, then knelt beside him. "You followed the rule and rescued the crop," she said quietly. "That is harder than accomplishing only one of those things."
What is the main problem Kai faces in the story?

["He must repair the solar panels before Dr. Osei returns.","He must save the freezing plants without breaking the rule about the heater.","He must find Pip, who has rolled away during the alarm.","He must convince his family to move back to Earth."]
The heater fails and the plants will freeze in forty minutes, but only adults may touch the heater and Dr. Osei cannot be reached. Kai has to protect the crop while still following the rule.

"Where's Dr. Osei?" Kai asked.

"Dr. Osei is outside repairing the solar panels. She will not return for two hours."

Kai's heart pounded like a drum. He was not permitted to touch the heater, and the rule was printed in enormous red letters across the control panel: AUTHORIZED ADULTS ONLY.

He pressed the radio button. "Dr. Osei, the greenhouse heater is broken! What should I do?"

Only static answered, because the solar panels were located on the far side of the crater, out of range.

Kai studied the drooping plants. Those beans were not merely plants; they were dinner for forty people next month. He considered breaking the rule, and then he considered another possibility.

"Pip," he said, "the plants need heat, not necessarily the heater. What else in here produces heat?"

Pip's light flickered while it searched its files. "Grow lamps produce heat. Section A lamps are currently off for the night cycle."

Kai grinned, because switching on grow lamps was one of his regular daily responsibilities. Together, he and Pip dragged the tall lamp stands from Section A into Section B and switched them on, and warm orange light spilled across the leaves.

Kai watched the thermometer anxiously. For ten long minutes, the number barely moved, but then it crept upward one degree, then two.

When Dr. Osei finally hurried through the airlock, she discovered Kai asleep against a lamp stand, with Pip parked beside him like a loyal dog. Every bean plant was standing tall.

She read the computer log, then knelt beside him. "You followed the rule and rescued the crop," she said quietly. "That is harder than accomplishing only one of those things."

The heater has failed and the temperature is falling, so the air in the dome is 'frigid,' which means very cold or freezing.

Pour a spoonful of sugar into a glass of warm water and stir. In a few seconds, the white grains seem to vanish. The water looks exactly as clear as it did before. Has the sugar disappeared? Scientists would say no, and they can prove it.

Everything around you is made of matter. Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Your desk, the air you breathe, and the water in your glass are all matter. Matter is built from particles that are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.

When sugar dissolves, its particles spread out evenly among the water particles. The sugar is still there, but the pieces are now too tiny and too scattered for your eyes to notice. A mixture like this, in which one substance spreads evenly through another, is called a solution.

One simple test shows that the sugar is still present. Take a small sip. The water now tastes sweet, so the sugar has not gone anywhere. Another test uses a scale. Weigh a cup of water and a spoonful of sugar separately, and add the two numbers. Next, stir the sugar into the water and weigh the mixture. The total weight stays the same. Even though the sugar can no longer be seen, every particle is still counted.

Scientists call this idea conservation of matter. It means that when substances mix, melt, freeze, or dissolve, the total amount of matter stays the same. Particles can move around and change position, but they do not simply vanish.

You can even get the sugar back. If you leave the sugar water in a sunny window for several days, the water will slowly evaporate into the air. As the water leaves, the sugar particles crowd closer together. Eventually, small crystals form on the bottom of the glass. The sugar was there the whole time, waiting.

Not every substance dissolves, however. Stir sand into water, and the grains will sink to the bottom. Sand and water make a mixture, but not a solution, because the sand does not spread out evenly.

So the next time something seems to disappear, think like a scientist. Ask yourself where its particles went. Chances are, the matter is still nearby, just hidden from view.

The whole passage explains that dissolved sugar is still present and that the total amount of matter stays the same. This idea is called conservation of matter.

In December of 1777, the American Revolution was not going well for the Continental Army. British soldiers had captured Philadelphia, the largest city in the colonies. General George Washington needed a safe place for his tired troops to spend the winter. He chose Valley Forge, a windy area of hills about twenty miles from the city.

When the army marched in on December 19, about twelve thousand soldiers arrived. Many had no shoes. Some left bloody footprints in the snow. Their first job was to build shelter. Working in small groups, the men cut down trees and built wooden huts. Each hut was about fourteen feet long and held twelve soldiers. Within a few weeks, a small city of logs stood on the frozen hills.

The huts kept out the wind, but they could not solve every problem. Food and clothing were hard to find. Farmers often preferred to sell their crops to the British, who paid in silver coins instead of paper money. On some days, soldiers ate only firecake, a plain mix of flour and water baked on hot stones. Even worse, diseases spread quickly through the crowded camp. About two thousand soldiers died that winter, mostly from illness rather than cold.

Then, in February of 1778, help arrived in an unusual form. A Prussian officer named Baron Friedrich von Steuben came to camp. He spoke very little English, yet he knew a great deal about training an army. Steuben began drilling a small group of soldiers. He taught them to march in step, to load their muskets quickly, and to charge together. Those soldiers then taught others. Before long, the whole army was practicing the same skills.

The change was remarkable. The soldiers who had stumbled into Valley Forge in December marched out in June as a stronger, more confident army. Only days later, they fought the British at the Battle of Monmouth in New Jersey. The fight ended without a clear winner, but the Americans held their ground against well-trained British troops.

Today, many historians consider Valley Forge a turning point in the war. No major battle was fought there; instead, the army won a quieter victory. It survived a terrible winter and learned to fight as one.

Picture a schoolyard where students pull carrots from the ground, chase butterflies between rows of sunflowers, and taste a tomato still warm from the sun. I believe every elementary school in the United States should have a garden like this. A school garden costs very little, and it teaches lessons that no textbook can.

First, gardens make science come alive. In class, students read that plants need water, air, and light to grow. In a garden, they see it happen. When students forget to water their bean plants for a week, they watch the leaves droop and turn yellow. That lesson sticks far better than a page in a book. Gardens also show how living things depend on one another. Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, and worms loosen the soil so roots can spread.

Second, gardens help children eat better. Many kids refuse to touch vegetables at dinner. Yet something surprising happens when they grow the vegetables themselves. Teachers across the country report that students who plant and harvest lettuce are much more willing to eat a salad. Pride, it seems, is a powerful seasoning.

Third, gardens teach responsibility and teamwork. A garden cannot be finished in one afternoon. Someone must water it, pull weeds, and protect it from hungry rabbits. Students learn to make schedules, share jobs, and keep promises to one another. If one group slacks off, everyone can see the result.

Some people argue that schools do not have enough space or money for gardens. This concern is understandable, but it is not a good reason to give up. A garden does not need to be large. A few wooden boxes along a sunny wall can grow herbs, peppers, and strawberries. Many local hardware stores and garden clubs are happy to donate seeds, soil, and tools. Parents and grandparents often volunteer their time, too.

Others worry that gardening takes time away from reading and math. In fact, gardens can strengthen those subjects. Students measure how tall their plants grow, keep journals about what they observe, and calculate how many seeds fit in each row.

A school garden is more than a patch of dirt. It is a classroom without walls. Let's give every child the chance to dig in.
What is the author's main claim?

["Every elementary school should have a garden because it teaches valuable lessons.","Students should grow all the food served in school lunches.","Only schools with large yards should have gardens.","Schools should replace science textbooks with gardening tools."]
In the first paragraph the author writes, 'I believe every elementary school in the United States should have a garden like this,' and the rest of the article gives reasons to support that claim.

Picture a schoolyard where students pull carrots from the ground, chase butterflies between rows of sunflowers, and taste a tomato still warm from the sun. I believe every elementary school in the United States should have a garden like this. A school garden costs very little, and it teaches lessons that no textbook can.

First, gardens make science come alive. In class, students read that plants need water, air, and light to grow. In a garden, they see it happen. When students forget to water their bean plants for a week, they watch the leaves droop and turn yellow. That lesson sticks far better than a page in a book. Gardens also show how living things depend on one another. Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, and worms loosen the soil so roots can spread.

Second, gardens help children eat better. Many kids refuse to touch vegetables at dinner. Yet something surprising happens when they grow the vegetables themselves. Teachers across the country report that students who plant and harvest lettuce are much more willing to eat a salad. Pride, it seems, is a powerful seasoning.

Third, gardens teach responsibility and teamwork. A garden cannot be finished in one afternoon. Someone must water it, pull weeds, and protect it from hungry rabbits. Students learn to make schedules, share jobs, and keep promises to one another. If one group slacks off, everyone can see the result.

Some people argue that schools do not have enough space or money for gardens. This concern is understandable, but it is not a good reason to give up. A garden does not need to be large. A few wooden boxes along a sunny wall can grow herbs, peppers, and strawberries. Many local hardware stores and garden clubs are happy to donate seeds, soil, and tools. Parents and grandparents often volunteer their time, too.

Others worry that gardening takes time away from reading and math. In fact, gardens can strengthen those subjects. Students measure how tall their plants grow, keep journals about what they observe, and calculate how many seeds fit in each row.

["Children should add more salt and pepper to their salads.","Children enjoy vegetables more when they have grown the vegetables themselves.","Children feel proud when they cook dinner for their families.","Children who garden become better at cooking than adults."]
A seasoning makes food taste better. The author says that students who plant and harvest lettuce are more willing to eat salad, so pride in their own work makes the vegetables more appealing.
