In the sentence "If one group slacks off, everyone can see the result," what does SLACKS OFF mean?
["trades jobs with another group","stops working as hard as it should","finishes its work early","asks for help from adults"]
The paragraph is about responsibility: watering, weeding, and keeping promises. If a group 'slacks off,' it does not do its share, and the garden shows the result.
The words INSPECT, SPECTATOR, and SPECTACLES all share the root SPECT. What does SPECT most likely mean?
To inspect is to look closely, a spectator watches an event, and spectacles help people see. The Latin root spect means 'to look.'
What does the prefix in MISUNDERSTAND mean?
The prefix mis- means 'wrongly' or 'badly.' To misunderstand is to understand something wrongly.
Which phrase best explains the meaning of DEPENDABLE?
["without any help","full of worry","able to be trusted","in a slow way"]
The suffix -able means 'able to be.' Dependable means able to be depended on, or trusted.
The Greek root GRAPH appears in AUTOGRAPH, PARAGRAPH, and PHOTOGRAPH. What does GRAPH mean?

An autograph is a person's own written name, a paragraph is a section of writing, and a photograph is 'drawn' with light. Graph means 'write or draw.' (Auto means 'self,' phon means 'sound,' and tele means 'far.')
TRANSPORT, PORTABLE, and EXPORT share the Latin root PORT. What does PORT mean?
To transport is to carry across, something portable can be carried, and exports are goods carried out of a country. Port means 'carry.'
Which word is a SYNONYM for ENORMOUS?
Enormous means extremely large, so huge is a synonym. Tiny is an antonym.
Which word is a SYNONYM for RELUCTANT?
A reluctant person does not want to do something. Unwilling has the same meaning; eager is the opposite.
Which word is an ANTONYM for FRAGILE?
Fragile means easily broken. Sturdy means strong and hard to break, so it is the opposite. Delicate and breakable are synonyms.
Which word is an ANTONYM for ANCIENT?
Ancient means very old, from long ago. Modern means new or of the present time, so it is the opposite.
Read the sentence: "The desert is so ARID that it may not rain there for months." What does ARID mean?
The clue 'it may not rain there for months' shows that arid means very dry.
Read the sentence: "After running the long race, Marcus was so EXHAUSTED that he fell asleep on the bus." What does EXHAUSTED mean?
Running a long race and then falling asleep are clues that exhausted means extremely tired.
Read the sentence: "Before the experiment, Lena wrote her HYPOTHESIS: 'I think the plant in the sunny window will grow taller.'" What is a HYPOTHESIS?
["a list of supplies","a final result","a prediction that can be tested","a drawing of a plant"]
Lena writes 'I think...' before the experiment begins. A hypothesis is a prediction, or educated guess, that an experiment can test.
In which sentence does WIND mean "to turn or twist something around"?
["We could hear the WIND whistling through the trees.","The WIND blew the leaves across the yard.","A cold WIND came down from the mountains.","Please WIND the yarn into a tight ball."]
Only 'WIND the yarn into a ball' uses wind as a verb meaning to turn or twist. In the other sentences, wind is a noun meaning moving air.
Read the sentence: "The principal will PRESENT the trophy at the assembly." What does PRESENT mean in this sentence?
["in attendance; not absent","to hand over formally","a gift for a birthday","the time happening now"]
Here present is a verb: the principal will give, or hand over, the trophy in a formal way. The other choices are different meanings of the same spelling.
Read the sentence: "The nurse cleaned the WOUND on my knee and covered it with a bandage." What does WOUND mean?
["a loud sound","turned around something","a small hill","an injury"]
A nurse cleans and bandages an injury, so wound means an injury in this sentence. 'Turned around something' is the meaning of wound (rhymes with sound), the past tense of wind.
On the first day of camp, the counselor played a silly game to BREAK THE ICE. What does BREAK THE ICE mean?
["crack a frozen pond","end a game early","cool down a hot room","help people feel relaxed when they first meet"]
The idiom 'break the ice' means to do something that helps people feel comfortable when they first meet.
"I have a spelling test tomorrow, so I need to HIT THE BOOKS tonight." What does HIT THE BOOKS mean?
["buy new books","go to the library","study hard","throw books on the floor"]
The idiom 'hit the books' means to study. The clue is the spelling test the next day.
Diego said the math quiz was A PIECE OF CAKE. What did he mean?
["The quiz was about fractions of a cake.","The quiz was very short.","The quiz was very easy.","The quiz made him hungry."]
The idiom 'a piece of cake' means something is very easy to do.
What is the meaning of the proverb DON'T COUNT YOUR CHICKENS BEFORE THEY HATCH?

["Don't depend on something good happening until it really happens.","Always take good care of animals on a farm.","Count carefully so that you do not make mistakes.","Be patient while you wait for spring to come."]
Eggs might not all hatch, so counting chickens early is a mistake. The proverb warns not to rely on a result before it actually happens.
What does the saying THE EARLY BIRD CATCHES THE WORM mean?
["People who start early have a better chance of success.","It is unwise to wake up before sunrise.","Birds are hungriest early in the morning.","People should share what they find with others."]
The bird that wakes up first gets the worm. The saying means that people who act early get an advantage.
What does the adage ACTIONS SPEAK LOUDER THAN WORDS mean?

["People who talk a lot are usually very active.","What you do shows more about you than what you say.","It is better to stay quiet than to give an opinion.","You should always speak in a loud voice."]
The adage means that a person's actions prove what they really think or feel better than their words do.
Complete the analogy. HOT is to COLD as TALL is to ______.
Hot and cold are opposites. The opposite of tall is short. High and large have meanings similar to tall, not opposite.
Complete the analogy. PETAL is to FLOWER as PAGE is to ______.
A petal is one part of a flower, and a page is one part of a book. This is a part-to-whole relationship.
Complete the analogy. AUTHOR is to NOVEL as COMPOSER is to ______.
An author creates a novel, and a composer creates a symphony. The relationship is creator to the thing created.
Your teacher asks you to ANALYZE a poem. What should you do?
["study its parts carefully to understand how it works","copy it neatly into your notebook","memorize it and say it out loud","write a new poem with a different topic"]
To analyze means to examine something closely by looking at its parts and how they work together.
When you SUMMARIZE a story, what do you do?
["retell only the most important ideas in a few sentences","change the ending to make it better","retell every detail in the exact order","explain whether you liked the story"]
A summary briefly states the main ideas and key events without all the small details or your opinions.
Read the sentence: "The scientist repeated the test three times to CONFIRM her results." What does CONFIRM mean?
["hide something from others","make sure something is true","forget about something","change something completely"]
Repeating a test helps a scientist make sure the results are correct. Confirm means to show or make sure that something is true.
The recipe says to PREHEAT the oven. What does PREHEAT mean?
["heat too much","heat again","not heat at all","heat before using"]
The prefix pre- means 'before.' To preheat the oven is to heat it before putting the food in.
Which word would best replace WALKED in this sentence? "With no plan at all, the tourists WALKED slowly through the market, looking at whatever caught their eye."
Wandered means walked slowly without a set plan or direction, which matches 'with no plan at all.' Marched, raced, and stomped describe walking with purpose, speed, or force.
The words BIOLOGY, BIOGRAPHY, and ANTIBIOTIC all contain the Greek root BIO. What does BIO mean?
Biology is the study of living things, a biography is the story of a person's life, and antibiotics fight living germs. Bio means 'life.' (The ending -logy means 'study.')

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"By the time we arrived at the theater, the movie ______."
["already starts","has already started","had already started","will have already started"]
The movie started before another past action (we arrived). The past perfect tense, 'had started,' shows the earlier of two past events.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Next June, my grandparents ______ married for fifty years."
'Next June' is a point in the future. The future perfect tense, 'will have been,' shows an action that will be complete by that future time.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Kenji ______ the piano since he was six, and he still practices every day."
The action began in the past and continues now ('he still practices'). The present perfect tense, 'has played,' is used with 'since' for actions that continue to the present.
Which sentence uses the past perfect tense correctly?

["After Lily will have finished her homework, she went outside to play.","After Lily had finished her homework, she went outside to play.","After Lily had finish her homework, she went outside to play.","After Lily has finished her homework, she went outside to play."]
The past perfect is formed with 'had' plus the past participle ('had finished'). It shows that finishing homework happened before going outside.
Which sentence has an inappropriate shift in verb tense?

["Yesterday Omar walked to the park and played soccer with his cousins.","Tomorrow Omar will walk to the park and play soccer with his cousins.","Every Saturday Omar walks to the park and plays soccer with his cousins.","Yesterday Omar walked to the park and plays soccer with his cousins."]
'Yesterday' tells us the actions happened in the past, so both verbs should be past tense. 'Walked' is past, but 'plays' shifts to present tense for no reason.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Last summer, we hiked up the mountain and ______ lunch at the top."
'Last summer' and 'hiked' are in the past tense, so the second verb must also be past tense: 'ate.'

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Our dog barks loudly whenever someone ______ the doorbell."
'Barks' and 'whenever' describe something that happens regularly in the present, so the verb should also be present tense: 'rings.'

Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence.
"You can have ______ pizza ______ tacos for dinner, but not both."
["both / and","either / or","neither / nor","not only / but also"]
'But not both' tells us there is a choice between two things. The correlative conjunction pair 'either...or' shows a choice.

Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence.
"______ my brother ______ my sister likes spinach, so we never cook it."
'We never cook it' shows that no one likes spinach. 'Neither' must be paired with 'nor.'

Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence.
"Mia is ______ a talented singer ______ a skilled dancer."
["not only / or","either / but also","neither / and","not only / but also"]
'Not only' is always paired with 'but also.' The sentence means Mia is good at both singing and dancing.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Neither the students nor the teacher ______ ready for the surprise fire drill."
With 'neither...nor,' the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. 'Teacher' is singular, so the verb is 'was.'

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Either the twins or their mother ______ going to pick us up after practice."
With 'either...or,' the verb agrees with the closer subject. 'Mother' is singular, so the verb is 'is.'

Which word in the sentence is an interjection?
"Wow, that rainbow has so many bright colors!"
An interjection is a word that expresses strong feeling or surprise. 'Wow' shows surprise and is set apart by a comma.
Which sentence correctly punctuates the interjection?
["Ouch. that pan is hot.","Ouch, That pan is hot.","Ouch! That pan is hot.","Ouch that pan is hot."]
A strong interjection can be followed by an exclamation point, and the next sentence begins with a capital letter. The other choices are missing punctuation or use capital letters incorrectly.
Which sentence uses a comma correctly after an introductory phrase?

["After the long hike we, rested beside the stream.","After the long hike, we rested beside the stream.","After the long, hike we rested beside the stream.","After, the long hike we rested beside the stream."]
The introductory phrase is 'After the long hike.' The comma belongs right after the whole phrase, before the main clause 'we rested beside the stream.'
["Yes I would love, to come to your party.","Yes, I would love to come to your party.","Yes I, would love to come to your party.","Yes I would love to come, to your party."]
A comma is used to set off the word 'yes' or 'no' at the beginning of a sentence.
Which sentence correctly uses a comma before a tag question?
["You finished your science project, didn't you?","You finished, your science project didn't you?","You finished your science, project didn't you?","You finished your science project didn't, you?"]
A tag question such as 'didn't you?' at the end of a sentence is set off with a comma.
Which sentence correctly uses commas to set off a person being spoken to?

["Thank you Ms. Rivera for helping us with the play.","Thank you, Ms. Rivera for helping us with the play.","Thank you, Ms. Rivera, for helping us with the play.","Thank you Ms., Rivera for helping us with the play."]
When a name in direct address comes in the middle of a sentence, commas go both before and after it.
["Is that your, backpack Sam?","Is that your backpack Sam?","Is that, your backpack Sam?","Is that your backpack, Sam?"]
Sam is being spoken to directly, so his name is set off from the rest of the sentence with a comma.
Which sentence correctly punctuates the title of a song?

["Our class sang This Land Is Your Land at the assembly.","Our class sang \"This Land\" Is Your Land at the assembly.","Our class sang \"This Land Is Your Land\" at the assembly.","Our class \"sang This Land Is Your Land\" at the assembly."]
Titles of short works such as songs, poems, and short stories are placed in quotation marks. The quotation marks must surround the whole title and only the title.
When you write the title of a BOOK by hand, what should you do?
["write it in all capital letters","put it in parentheses","underline it","put it in quotation marks"]
Titles of long works, such as books and movies, are italicized when typed and underlined when written by hand.
Which of these titles should be placed in quotation marks instead of being underlined or italicized?
["a short poem in a poetry collection","a long novel","a monthly magazine","a full-length movie"]
Short works, such as a single poem, go in quotation marks. Long works, such as novels, movies, and magazines, are underlined or italicized.

Which word in the sentence is a preposition?
"The kite drifted above the tall trees."
A preposition shows the relationship between a noun and another word. 'Above' shows where the kite drifted in relation to the trees.

Choose the preposition that correctly completes the sentence.
"Ava is very interested ______ learning about volcanoes."
In standard English, we say someone is 'interested in' something.

Choose the preposition that correctly completes the sentence.
"The library is ______ the bakery and the post office."
'Between' is used to show a position in the middle of two things: the bakery and the post office. 'Among' is used for three or more.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"The box of crayons ______ on the top shelf."
The subject is 'box,' which is singular. 'Of crayons' is a prepositional phrase and does not change the subject, so the verb is 'is.'

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Each of the players ______ a new jersey for the championship game."
'Each' is singular, even when it is followed by 'of the players.' So the singular verb 'has' is correct.

Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"The news about the storm ______ worrying everyone in town."
'News' ends in -s but is a singular noun. The singular verb 'is' agrees with it.

Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"Grandpa took Leo and ______ to the aquarium on Saturday."
The pronoun is an object of the verb 'took.' Try it alone: 'Grandpa took me,' not 'Grandpa took I.' So 'me' is correct.

Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"______ and Ella built the robot for the science club."
The pronoun is part of the subject of the sentence. Try it alone: 'She built the robot,' not 'Her built the robot.' So 'She' is correct.

When Ms. Okafor posted the debate assignments on the classroom door, Priya read her name twice to make sure there was no mistake. The question for the sixth-grade tournament was whether the town should convert the empty lot on Birch Avenue into a parking garage. Priya had spent the entire fall collecting signatures to transform that lot into a neighborhood park, yet she had been assigned to argue in favor of the garage.

"This has to be an error," she protested after class. "Everyone knows my opinion."

Nadia had planned her science fair project down to the last detail. She would grow bean plants under three colors of light, red, blue, and green, and demonstrate that blue light produced the tallest, healthiest plants. Three articles had predicted exactly that result, so all she needed was the evidence.

For four weeks she measured her plants every afternoon and recorded each height in a spiral notebook. Then, during the third week, the plants under the blue bulb began to droop, and their leaves turned pale yellow and curled at the edges. By the end of the month, the tallest plants on the shelf were the ones under red light, while the blue plants looked as if they had given up.

Nadia stared at her notebook in dismay. The fair was only four days away, and her results were the complete opposite of her prediction.

"Just leave out the blue plants," suggested her brother, Karim. "Say something broke and show the other two."

"That would be dishonest," Nadia answered, although she did not sound entirely certain.

That evening she sat beside the shelf with a flashlight, examining every part of her setup for a clue. The soil was moist, and the timers on the lamps were working properly. Then she held her hand beneath the blue lamp and immediately pulled it away. She had purchased that bulb at a different store, and it was an older type that produced a tremendous amount of heat. Her plants had not suffered because of the color of the light; they had been cooked.

Since there was no time to repeat the experiment, Nadia decided to do something that felt risky. She rewrote her poster, and across the top, in large letters, she printed "What Went Wrong, and What I Learned." Underneath, she explained her hypothesis, displayed every measurement, described the overheated bulb, and listed how she would control the temperature in a future experiment.

At the fair, one judge studied the poster silently for a long time while Nadia's palms grew damp. At last the judge looked up. "Do you know how many professional scientists make a mistake like this?" she asked. "Most of them, and the good ones write it down."

Nadia did not win first place, but she received an honorable mention. The judge's card, which she pinned above her desk, said simply, "Honest work."
Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?

["Honesty about mistakes is part of doing good science.","First place is the only reward that matters at a science fair.","Following a careful plan always guarantees the expected result.","Brothers and sisters should help each other with schoolwork."]
Nadia reports her failed results honestly and is praised for it by the judge. The story shows that careful plans can still go wrong, and Karim's advice is rejected.

By the spring of 1935, dust had been blowing across the Oklahoma plains for four long years, and twelve-year-old Ruth Dawson could hardly remember the color of growing wheat. Every morning she swept a gray film off the kitchen table, and by evening it had always returned. Her mother hung damp sheets over the windows and stuffed rags beneath the doors, but the powdery dust still crept inside, settling in the flour bin and in the folds of the blankets.

On a Sunday afternoon in April, the northern sky turned black. It was not an ordinary rain cloud but an enormous wall of dirt, hundreds of feet high, rolling toward the farm faster than a train. While the wind howled for hours, the family huddled in the dark kitchen with wet cloths pressed over their faces. When the storm finally ended, drifts of soil were piled against the barn like brown snow.

That night Ruth overheard her parents talking quietly at the table. Her uncle had written from California, where he was picking fruit, to report that there was steady work and the sky was always blue.

"We could leave next month," her mother said.

Ruth held her breath. Part of her wanted to go, because she was tired of grit between her teeth and of watching her father's shoulders sag as he walked through the ruined fields.

However, her father shook his head. "A man from the county office visited last week," he explained. "He says the soil blew away because farmers plowed up the prairie grass that used to hold it in place. The government will pay us to plow in curves along the hills and to plant rows of trees that slow the wind. If enough families cooperate, the land might recover."

"Might," her mother repeated.

"Might," he agreed.

They stayed. That autumn, Ruth and her father planted a line of thin cedar and elm seedlings along the edge of the north field. They hauled water from the well in heavy buckets, yet many of the young trees withered anyway, and Ruth decided the work was hopeless.

The following spring, however, she noticed tiny new leaves on the trees that had survived. Ruth knelt beside the nearest one and touched a leaf gently, as if it might blow away. For the first time in years, she allowed herself to imagine the field full of wheat.
Which statement best summarizes the story?

["A girl learns that the dust storms on the plains are much less dangerous than most people believe.","A farm family survives years of dust storms and, through patient work, begins to hope again.","A farmer discovers that wheat grows best when it is planted in curved rows along the hills.","A farm family decides to move to California, where an uncle has found steady work picking fruit."]
The family stays, plants trees, and at the end Ruth sees new leaves and imagines wheat again. They do not move, and the other choices are not supported.

A honeybee colony can contain more than forty thousand bees, but only some of them are foragers, the workers that fly out to collect nectar and pollen. When a forager finds a rich patch of flowers, the whole colony benefits if others can find it too. But how can a tiny insect tell her sisters where to fly? The answer is one of the most remarkable discoveries about animal behavior: bees dance.

In the 1940s, an Austrian scientist named Karl von Frisch spent years watching bees inside glass-walled hives. He noticed that a forager returning with food would often move in a strange pattern on the honeycomb. She would walk forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circle back and repeat the movement. Von Frisch called this the "waggle dance."

Through careful experiments, he found that the dance contains a kind of code. The direction of the straight "waggle run" tells other bees which way to fly. The comb inside the hive hangs in a vertical position, and it is too dark to see the sky. So the dancer uses "straight up" on the comb to stand for the direction of the sun. If she waggles straight up, the flowers are toward the sun. If she waggles at an angle to the right of straight up, the flowers lie at that same angle to the right of the sun.

The length of the waggle run tells how far away the food is. A short run means the flowers are close, while a longer run signals a longer trip. Other bees crowd around the dancer and follow her movements with their antennae. They also smell the scent of the flowers on her body. Then they leave the hive and head for the spot she has described.

At first, many scientists doubted that an insect could share such detailed information. Later, researchers tested the idea by attaching tiny tags to bees and following their flights with radar. The tracks showed that bees that had watched a dance really did fly in the direction it described.

Von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize for his work in 1973. His discovery also matters today. Farmers depend on honeybees to pollinate crops such as apples and almonds. By understanding how bees find food, scientists can protect these insects and the harvests that rely on them.

For more than a thousand years, a network of trade routes connected China with the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. Today we call this network the Silk Road, even though it was not a single road and it carried much more than silk.

The name comes from China's most famous export. For centuries, the Chinese kept the method of making silk a closely guarded secret. Wealthy people as far away as Rome prized the smooth, shimmering cloth and paid enormous prices for it. In return, goods such as glass, silver, wool, and horses traveled east toward China.

Very few traders ever traveled the entire route, which stretched about four thousand miles. Instead, goods moved from one merchant to the next, a little like a baton in a relay race. A bolt of silk might change hands a dozen times before it reached a market in the west. Each merchant added to the price to earn a profit, so by the end of the journey the cloth cost far more than it had at the start.

The journey was difficult and often dangerous. Caravans crossed burning deserts, such as the Taklamakan, and climbed through freezing mountain passes. Traders depended on camels, which could carry heavy loads and go for days without water. Along the main routes, travelers stopped at inns called caravanserais. These walled inns were spaced about a day's journey apart, and they offered food, water, and a safe place to sleep.

Perhaps the most important cargo on the Silk Road could not be packed into a saddlebag. Ideas, beliefs, and inventions traveled with the merchants. Buddhism spread from India into China along these routes. The knowledge of how to make paper slowly moved west from China and eventually reached Europe. Foods such as grapes, peaches, and spices found new homes far from where they were first grown. Sadly, not everything that spread was welcome. Diseases also moved along the trade routes, sometimes with deadly results.

In time, ships began to carry more goods by sea, and the overland routes became less important. Still, the Silk Road had shown that trade does more than move objects. When people exchange goods, they also exchange ideas, and those ideas can change the world.

In 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener proposed an idea that most experts thought was ridiculous. He claimed that all of the continents had once been joined together in one giant landmass, which he later called Pangaea. Over millions of years, he said, the pieces had slowly drifted apart.

Wegener did not invent this idea out of thin air. He had collected several kinds of evidence. First, he pointed out that the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a puzzle. Second, fossils of the same plants and animals had been found on continents now separated by wide oceans. One example was Mesosaurus, a small reptile that lived in fresh water. Its fossils appear in both Brazil and southern Africa, yet it could never have swum across a salty ocean. Third, he found signs that glaciers had once covered parts of Africa and India, places that are hot today.

Even so, most scientists rejected his idea. The main problem was that Wegener could not explain what force was strong enough to push entire continents. He suggested that the continents plowed through the rocky ocean floor like ships through ice, but other experts showed that this was impossible. Without a believable cause, they refused to accept his theory. Wegener kept gathering evidence until he died on a research trip to Greenland in 1930.

The answer came from the bottom of the sea. In the 1950s and 1960s, scientists used sound waves to map the ocean floor. They discovered long underwater mountain ranges where hot rock rises from deep inside Earth. As this rock cools, it forms new ocean floor, which slowly spreads away from the ridge on both sides.

These discoveries led to the theory of plate tectonics. According to this theory, Earth's outer layer is broken into huge plates that move a few inches each year. The continents ride along on top of these plates. The theory also explained why most earthquakes and volcanoes happen near the edges of the plates.

Today, Wegener is remembered as a scientist who was right about the big idea, even though he was wrong about how it worked. His story shows that science can change its mind when new evidence appears.

The passage traces Wegener's idea from rejection to acceptance as part of plate tectonics. The other choices are minor details or are contradicted by the text.

Wegener did not invent this idea out of thin air. He had collected several kinds of evidence. First, he pointed out that the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a puzzle. Second, fossils of the same plants and animals had been found on continents now separated by wide oceans. One example was Mesosaurus, a small reptile that lived in fresh water. Its fossils appear in both Brazil and southern Africa, yet it could never have swum across a salty ocean. Third, he found signs that glaciers had once covered parts of Africa and India, places that are hot today.

Even so, most scientists rejected his idea. The main problem was that Wegener could not explain what force was strong enough to push entire continents. He suggested that the continents plowed through the rocky ocean floor like ships through ice, but other experts showed that this was impossible. Without a believable cause, they refused to accept his theory. Wegener kept gathering evidence until he died on a research trip to Greenland in 1930.

The answer came from the bottom of the sea. In the 1950s and 1960s, scientists used sound waves to map the ocean floor. They discovered long underwater mountain ranges where hot rock rises from deep inside Earth. As this rock cools, it forms new ocean floor, which slowly spreads away from the ridge on both sides.

These discoveries led to the theory of plate tectonics. According to this theory, Earth's outer layer is broken into huge plates that move a few inches each year. The continents ride along on top of these plates. The theory also explained why most earthquakes and volcanoes happen near the edges of the plates.

Today, Wegener is remembered as a scientist who was right about the big idea, even though he was wrong about how it worked. His story shows that science can change its mind when new evidence appears.
Why are Mesosaurus fossils strong evidence for Wegener's idea?

["Mesosaurus was a powerful swimmer that could cross wide oceans with ease.","Mesosaurus could not cross an ocean, so the two continents were likely once joined.","The fossils prove that glaciers once covered both Brazil and southern Africa.","The fossils show that reptiles were only able to live in very hot places."]
The passage says Mesosaurus lived in fresh water and could never have swum across a salty ocean, so finding it on both continents suggests they were joined.

Jada was so METICULOUS about her science notes that she labeled every diagram and checked each measurement twice. METICULOUS most nearly means
["fast but careless and sloppy","unwilling to share with others","extremely careful about details","easily bored by schoolwork"]
Labeling every diagram and checking each measurement twice shows great care about small details.
When the coach asked for CANDID feedback, Omar honestly admitted that the drills were too long and confusing. CANDID most nearly means
["angry and loud","polite but vague","secretive and hidden","open and truthful"]
Omar's honest admission is an example of candid, or frank and truthful, feedback.
Because Rosa was DILIGENT, she practiced the violin every day, even on weekends and holidays. DILIGENT most nearly means
["easily distracted by noise","talented by nature","hardworking and steady","nervous and fearful"]
Practicing every day, even on holidays, shows steady, careful effort, which is what diligent means.
Paper maps have not become completely OBSOLETE; many hikers still carry one in case their electronic devices lose power. OBSOLETE most nearly means
["small and light enough to carry","out of date and no longer used","difficult for most people to read","too expensive for most people"]
The sentence says paper maps are still used, so they are not completely out of date; obsolete means no longer in use.
With dark clouds rolling in and thunder getting louder, it seemed INEVITABLE that the picnic would be canceled. INEVITABLE most nearly means
["pleasant and fun","surprising to everyone","unlikely to happen","certain to happen"]
The growing storm made the cancellation unavoidable, so inevitable means certain to happen.
Lucas HESITATED at the edge of the diving board, wondering whether the water was too deep, before he finally jumped. HESITATED most nearly means
["laughed nervously","paused because he was unsure","shouted loudly to his friends","slipped suddenly on the board"]
Lucas waits while he wonders about the water before jumping, so hesitated means paused out of uncertainty.
One CONSEQUENCE of leaving the freezer door open overnight was a puddle of melted ice cream on the floor. CONSEQUENCE most nearly means
The puddle happened because the door was left open, so it is a result, or consequence.
Which word is an ANTONYM of VAGUE?
Vague means unclear or not specific; precise means exact and clear. Unclear and fuzzy are synonyms.
Which word is a SYNONYM of CEASE?
To cease is to come to an end, so stop is the synonym; begin is the antonym.
Which word is an ANTONYM of TRANQUIL?
Tranquil means calm and quiet; chaotic means wild and disordered. Peaceful and calm are synonyms.
The students built an ELABORATE model of the solar system, with moving planets, tiny moons, and lights that blinked on and off. ELABORATE most nearly means
["old and worn out","plain and simple","small and cheaply made","detailed and complex"]
The model has many detailed parts (moving planets, moons, blinking lights), so elaborate means detailed and complicated.
The words CREDIBLE, INCREDIBLE, and CREDENTIALS share the Latin root CRED, which means
Cred means believe: a credible story can be believed, and an incredible one is hard to believe.
The prefix SEMI- in SEMICIRCLE means
Semi- means half, so a semicircle is half of a circle.
The prefix ANTI- in ANTIBACTERIAL means
Anti- means against; an antibacterial soap works against bacteria.
The words PROJECT, EJECT, and REJECT share the Latin root JECT, which means
Ject means throw: to eject is to throw out, and a projector throws an image forward onto a screen.
The words EVACUATE, VACANT, and VACUUM share the Latin root VAC, which means
Vac means empty: a vacant lot is empty, and to evacuate a building is to empty it of people.
The prefix TRANS- in TRANSCONTINENTAL means
Trans- means across; a transcontinental railroad runs across a continent.
The prefix CIRCUM- in CIRCUMNAVIGATE means
Circum- means around; to circumnavigate is to sail all the way around something, such as the earth.
The words MANUAL, MANUFACTURE, and MANUSCRIPT share the Latin root MANU, which means
Manu means hand: manual work is done by hand, and a manuscript was originally written by hand.
In the word GEOLOGIST, the suffix -IST means
["full of or having","a person who does or studies","in the direction of","the study or science of"]
-ist names a person: a geologist studies rocks and the earth, and a cyclist rides a bicycle. The study of is -logy.
In which sentence does CHARGE mean "to rush forward in an attack"?

["The store will CHARGE five dollars for a small bag of popcorn.","Remember to CHARGE your tablet before the field trip.","Ms. Lee put Andre in CHARGE of feeding the class hamster.","The bull lowered its head and began to CHARGE."]
A bull that lowers its head and charges is rushing forward to attack. The other sentences use charge to mean ask a price, fill with electricity, and responsibility.
"The class will CONDUCT an experiment to see which paper towel absorbs the most water." In this sentence, CONDUCT means
["behave","lead an orchestra","allow heat to pass through","carry out"]
Conduct has several meanings; to conduct an experiment is to carry it out or perform it.
In which sentence does PITCH mean "how high or low a sound is"?

["The campers helped PITCH the tent before dark.","Jada threw a fast PITCH, and the batter missed.","The night was so cloudy that the woods were PITCH black.","The singer's voice rose to a high PITCH at the end."]
Only the singer's voice refers to the highness of a sound. The others mean set up, a thrown ball, and very dark.
When the bridge they built from straws collapsed, the team sighed and said, "Well, it's BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD." This idiom means
["it is time to draw a picture of the bridge","the project is finished and was a success","they should give up on the project completely","it is time to start over with a new plan"]
The phrase means a plan has failed and must be redesigned from the beginning.
After Maya offered to trade her stickers, she told her friend, "THE BALL IS IN YOUR COURT." She means that
["her friend has already lost the game","her friend should go outside and play","it is her friend's turn to decide","the trade is already over and done"]
The idiom comes from tennis: once the ball is on your side, you must respond. Maya is waiting for her friend's decision.
Ben signed up for the talent show, but he GOT COLD FEET the night before and almost backed out. GOT COLD FEET means
["caught a cold from the winter weather","felt excited and confident","practiced late into the night","became too nervous to follow through"]
"Almost backed out" shows that Ben lost his courage; getting cold feet means becoming too nervous to follow through.
Each word below describes someone who refuses to give up. Which word has the most POSITIVE connotation?
Determined suggests admirable persistence. Stubborn, pigheaded, and obstinate suggest an unreasonable refusal to change.
["The bacon danced across the pan.","The bacon sizzled and popped in the hot pan.","The bacon was the best breakfast in the whole universe.","The bacon was as crispy as a dry autumn leaf."]
Sizzled and popped imitate the sounds they name, which is onomatopoeia. The others are a simile, hyperbole, and personification.
A caterpillar grows into a butterfly; a tadpole grows into a frog (young stage : adult).
A thermometer measures temperature; a scale measures weight (tool : what it measures). Height is measured with a ruler or tape.
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence: Either my cousins or my uncle ___ going to drive us to the airport.
With either...or, the verb agrees with the closer subject; "uncle" is singular, so "is" is correct.
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence: One of the windows in the art room ___ cracked.
The subject is "One," which is singular; the phrase "of the windows" does not change it, so the singular verb "is" is correct.
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence: The members of the robotics club ___ in the library every Thursday.
The subject is "members," which is plural, not "club" (the object of the preposition), so the plural verb "meet" is correct.
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence: There ___ several good reasons to start the project early.
In a sentence beginning with "There," the subject follows the verb; "reasons" is plural, so "are" is correct.
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: Our dog was so tired after the hike that he was ___ on the porch all afternoon.
To lie means to rest; its -ing form is "lying." Laying means placing something down, and "was lain" is incorrect.
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The surgeon worked ___ so that she would not make a single mistake.
The word describes how the surgeon worked (a verb), so the adverb "carefully" is needed.
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: Our team played ___ in the championship game, scoring four goals.
"Well" is the adverb that describes how the team played; "good" is an adjective and should not modify a verb.
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: Of the three puppies in the litter, Pepper is the ___.
When comparing three or more, use the superlative; for a short adjective, add -est: "smallest."
Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence: Today's hike up the ridge was ___ than last week's walk by the lake.
For a long adjective comparing two things, use "more" plus the adjective: "more difficult."
["We don't have no milk left for the cereal.","We don't have any milk left for the cereal.","We don't have hardly no milk left for the cereal.","We haven't got no milk left for the cereal."]
Using two negatives such as don't and no is a double negative. "Don't...any" is the standard form.
Choose the conjunction that best completes the sentence: Leah wanted to go swimming, ___ the pool was closed for cleaning.
The second clause contrasts with what Leah wanted, so the contrasting conjunction "but" fits.
Choose the word that best completes the sentence: ___ the field was muddy, the referees allowed the game to continue.
The game continued in spite of the mud, so "Although" shows the contrast. "Because" and "Since" would wrongly suggest the mud caused the game to continue.
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: Not only did Sam finish his own science project, ___ he also helped his younger sister with hers.
"Not only" is part of the correlative pair "not only...but (also)."
Choose the preposition that correctly completes the sentence: Jamal is responsible ___ feeding the class fish every morning.
The standard phrase is "responsible for" a task.
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The engineer ___ designed the new bridge spoke at our school assembly.
"Who" is the relative pronoun for a person acting as the subject of the clause ("who designed the bridge").
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: We met an author ___ latest book is about a girl who trains sled dogs.
"Whose" shows possession (the author's book). "Who's" means "who is."
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The student ___ the principal chose to give the welcome speech lives on my street.
The pronoun is the object of "chose" (the principal chose her), so the objective form "whom" is correct. "Which" is not used for people.
Which of the following is a sentence FRAGMENT?
["Because the bridge was closed for repairs.","The bridge was closed for repairs.","We took the long way because the bridge was closed.","Closed for repairs, the bridge stood empty."]
A clause beginning with "Because" is dependent and cannot stand alone; it needs an independent clause to complete the thought.
Which choice correctly fixes this fragment? Hoping to see the comet. We stayed up past midnight.

["Hoping to see the comet, we stayed up past midnight.","Hoping. To see the comet, we stayed up past midnight.","Hoping to see the comet. We stayed up, past midnight.","Hoping to see the comet we stayed. Up past midnight."]
Joining the phrase to the complete sentence with a comma creates one correct sentence with an introductory phrase.
Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?

["During spring break, my cousin and i toured the Statue of Liberty in New York harbor.","During Spring Break, my cousin and I toured the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor.","During spring break, my Cousin and I toured the statue of liberty in New York Harbor.","During spring break, my cousin and I toured the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor."]
The pronoun I and the names of specific places (Statue of Liberty, New York Harbor) are capitalized; seasons, school breaks, and "cousin" after "my" are not.
Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?

["We drove south for two days to visit Uncle Ray in georgia.","We drove south for two days to visit Uncle Ray in Georgia.","We drove south for two days to visit uncle Ray in Georgia.","We drove South for two days to visit Uncle Ray in Georgia."]
A direction used as a direction (drove south) is lowercase; a title used with a name (Uncle Ray) and a state name are capitalized.
Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?

["The two teacher's classrooms are across the hall from each other.","The two teachers's classrooms are across the hall from each other.","The two teachers classroom's are across the hall from each other.","The two teachers' classrooms are across the hall from each other."]
To show that something belongs to more than one teacher, add only an apostrophe after the plural -s: "teachers'." Plain plurals such as "classrooms" take no apostrophe.
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence: The natural history museum is famous for ___ huge collection of dinosaur fossils.
"Its" is the possessive pronoun. "It's" means "it is," and "its'" is not a word.
Which sentence uses a colon correctly?

["Please bring three supplies to: class, a pencil, an eraser, and a ruler.","Please bring three supplies to class: a pencil, an eraser, and a ruler.","Please: bring three supplies to class, a pencil, an eraser, and a ruler.","Please bring: a pencil, an eraser, and a ruler to class."]
A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence ("Please bring three supplies to class"). It should not split a verb from its object.

["\"Can you help me carry these boxes,\" asked Leo?","\"Can you help me carry these boxes?\" asked Leo.","\"Can you help me carry these boxes?,\" asked Leo.","\"Can you help me carry these boxes\"? asked Leo."]
The question mark belongs inside the closing quotation mark because the quotation itself is a question, and no extra comma is added.

["It was a cold, windy, night so we stayed inside, and played board games.","It was a cold, windy night, so we stayed inside and played board games.","It was a cold windy, night so we stayed inside and played board games.","It was, a cold windy night so, we stayed inside and played board games."]
Coordinate adjectives (cold, windy) are separated by a comma, and a comma comes before "so" when it joins two independent clauses.
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence: By the end of practice, Mia had ___ twenty laps in the pool.
After the helping verb "had," use the past participle; the past participle of swim is "swum."
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence: While Grandpa ___ the fence, a robin landed on the top of his ladder.
The past progressive "was painting" shows an action in progress when another past action (the robin landed) happened.
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence: By the time the guests arrive tonight, we ___ the entire house.
The future perfect "will have cleaned" shows an action that will be completed before a certain time in the future (before the guests arrive).

Every weekday morning at 7:15, Mrs. Alvarez settled onto the green bench beside the bus stop on Fulton Street. She never actually rode the bus; she simply sat with her hands folded on her cane and observed the commuters hurrying past without speaking.

Jonah noticed her only because he had no alternative. The bench was the only place to sit while he waited for the school bus, and she always occupied the left half of it. For the first two weeks of sixth grade, he stood instead, earbuds in, staring at the corner where the bus would appear.

On a gloomy Tuesday in October, the rain came down hard and sideways, and Jonah, who had forgotten his jacket, was trying to decide whether to sprint home when an enormous black umbrella tilted over his head.

"Sit," Mrs. Alvarez said. It was not a question.

He sat. The umbrella was large enough to shelter both of them, and it smelled faintly of cedar, like the inside of an old closet. Eventually she pointed her cane at a man in a gray suit who was jogging anxiously toward the train station.

"That one is late every Tuesday because his daughter has swim practice, and he drops her off first," she said.

Jonah stared at her and asked how she could possibly know that.

"I pay attention," she replied. "People will tell you their entire life stories if you watch them patiently enough."

Afterward, Jonah stopped wearing his earbuds at the bus stop. Mrs. Alvarez taught him to notice the baker who whistled the same three notes every morning and the girl with the cello case who always counted her steps. Jonah began inventing stories about each of them, and Mrs. Alvarez corrected him whenever he got the facts wrong.

In December, the bench remained empty for three days in a row. On the fourth day, Jonah knocked on the door of the yellow house where he had seen her go inside. Her nephew explained that she had fallen and was recovering in the hospital.

The next morning, Jonah sat on the left half of the bench and watched the man in the gray suit, the whistling baker, and the girl with the cello. That afternoon he wrote down everything he had observed, folded the paper twice, and carried it to the hospital so she would not miss a thing.
Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?

["Bad weather can ruin even the most carefully planned day.","Young people should always respect the rules set by older adults.","People who live alone usually prefer to keep to themselves.","Paying close attention to others can lead to unexpected and meaningful friendships."]
Jonah ignores the people around him until Mrs. Alvarez teaches him to watch closely; that habit grows into a caring friendship. The other choices are not developed by the story.

Every weekday morning at 7:15, Mrs. Alvarez settled onto the green bench beside the bus stop on Fulton Street. She never actually rode the bus; she simply sat with her hands folded on her cane and observed the commuters hurrying past without speaking.

Jonah noticed her only because he had no alternative. The bench was the only place to sit while he waited for the school bus, and she always occupied the left half of it. For the first two weeks of sixth grade, he stood instead, earbuds in, staring at the corner where the bus would appear.

On a gloomy Tuesday in October, the rain came down hard and sideways, and Jonah, who had forgotten his jacket, was trying to decide whether to sprint home when an enormous black umbrella tilted over his head.

"Sit," Mrs. Alvarez said. It was not a question.

He sat. The umbrella was large enough to shelter both of them, and it smelled faintly of cedar, like the inside of an old closet. Eventually she pointed her cane at a man in a gray suit who was jogging anxiously toward the train station.

"That one is late every Tuesday because his daughter has swim practice, and he drops her off first," she said.

Jonah stared at her and asked how she could possibly know that.

"I pay attention," she replied. "People will tell you their entire life stories if you watch them patiently enough."

Afterward, Jonah stopped wearing his earbuds at the bus stop. Mrs. Alvarez taught him to notice the baker who whistled the same three notes every morning and the girl with the cello case who always counted her steps. Jonah began inventing stories about each of them, and Mrs. Alvarez corrected him whenever he got the facts wrong.

The summer I turned eleven, my father announced that I would not be getting a new bicycle; instead, I would be repairing the old one.

The old one was a rusty red mountain bike that had belonged to my cousin, then to my older brother, and finally to me. Its chain squealed like an angry bird, and the back brake worked only when it felt like cooperating. I had been begging for a shiny new bike since April. My father listened patiently to every argument I made, nodded thoughtfully, and then handed me a wrench.

"A bike is just a puzzle," he said, "and you are perfectly capable of solving a puzzle."

I did not want to solve a puzzle; I wanted to ride. Since I had no other choice, however, I spent the first week of July sitting on the scorching driveway with a library book about bicycle repair open beside me. The diagrams looked simple, but the actual bicycle was far more complicated.

On the first day, I removed the back wheel and could not figure out how to reattach it. On the third day, I lost a tiny spring under the porch and spent an hour searching for it with a flashlight. On the fifth day, I tightened the brake cable so hard that the wheel refused to turn at all, and I collapsed onto the concrete and cried, partly from frustration and partly from the heat.

My father came outside and sat beside me, but he did not pick up the wrench. Instead, he asked me what I had learned so far. I listed everything that had gone wrong. He laughed and said, "That's not a list of mistakes. That's a list of things you know now."

By the end of July, the chain was silent and both brakes worked perfectly. The first time I coasted down Maple Hill, with the wind roaring in my ears, I felt as if I had built the bicycle myself from nothing.

I am an adult now, and I have owned many bicycles since then, but not one of them has mattered as much as that rusty red one. Whenever something in my life breaks, I still hear my father's voice reminding me that it is just a puzzle, and I still believe him.
What is the central idea of this narrative?

["Riding down a steep hill is the most exciting part of owning a bike.","Working through repeated mistakes taught the narrator patience and confidence that lasted into adulthood.","Library books are the best way to learn how to repair a bicycle.","The narrator's father was too strict to buy his child a new bicycle."]
The narrator struggles, learns from each failure, succeeds, and still uses the lesson as an adult. The other choices are minor details or unsupported opinions.

Every April, Theo and his older sister June constructed a kite together. They reused the same wooden frame every year, repaired with tape, and decorated it with whatever paper they could find. One year it was faded road maps, and another year it was the colorful comics from the Sunday newspaper. This year, June had covered it with pages from her old school notebooks, so the kite was crowded with her loopy handwriting and half-finished math problems.

"Last one," she said quietly, tying on the tail. In August she would be leaving for college, three states away.

Theo did not answer; he pretended to be extremely busy untangling the string.

They climbed to the top of Carver Hill, where the wind always blew steadily from the west. June ran first, as she always did, and the kite leaped into the air, wobbled uncertainly, and then climbed until it was a small bright square against the clouds. Theo watched the string grow tight as it hummed in the wind, a thin line connecting the hill to the sky.

After a while, June held the spool out to him and said, "You take it."

"But you always fly it," Theo protested.

"Not anymore," she said gently, nudging his elbow with encouragement.

He accepted the spool. The kite pulled harder than he expected, tugging at his arms as if it wanted to travel somewhere he could not follow, and for a moment he was afraid he would lose it. Then he discovered the rhythm, releasing a little string when the wind gusted and reeling it back when the wind calmed. If he held the string too tightly, it might snap, but if he held it too loosely, the kite would fall.

"See?" June remarked approvingly. "It's not about holding on as hard as you can."

In late August, the house felt unbearably quiet. One windy evening, Theo carried the kite up Carver Hill by himself, launched it on the second try, and let it climb higher than it had ever gone before. June's handwriting was too far away to read now, but he could feel the steady tug through the string, faint and patient, like someone on the other end saying hello.
In the story, the kite string most likely symbolizes

["the danger of playing outside on a windy day.","the bond between Theo and June that remains even when they are far apart.","the rules that Theo's parents expect him to follow.","the schoolwork June left unfinished before college."]
The string connects Theo to the kite (covered in June's handwriting); at the end its "tug" feels "like someone on the other end saying hello," showing a connection that survives distance.

More than five thousand years ago, some of the world's first cities grew up in a region called Mesopotamia. The name comes from Greek words meaning "the land between the rivers." The two rivers were the Tigris and the Euphrates, which flow through what is now Iraq. Although the region got little rain, the rivers made life there possible.

Each spring, melting snow in the northern mountains caused the rivers to flood. The floodwaters spread rich, dark soil across the land. However, the floods were hard to predict. Some years they came too late to help the crops, and other years they were strong enough to wash away whole villages. To control the water, farmers dug canals and built walls of earth called levees. This system of irrigation carried river water to fields that would otherwise have been too dry to farm.

Irrigation changed everything. Farmers could now grow more barley and wheat than their families needed. This extra food, called a surplus, meant that not everyone had to be a farmer. Some people became potters, weavers, metalworkers, or traders. Others became priests or leaders. As villages grew larger, they turned into city-states such as Ur and Uruk. Each city-state had its own ruler and its own temple, often a tall stepped tower called a ziggurat.

With so much trade and so many goods, people needed a way to keep track of who owned what. The Sumerians, who lived in southern Mesopotamia, solved this problem by creating one of the earliest known writing systems. At first, they pressed simple pictures into wet clay to record sheep or bags of grain. Over time, the pictures changed into wedge-shaped marks made with a cut reed. Today, this writing is called cuneiform, from a Latin word meaning "wedge."

Learning cuneiform was hard, so only a small group of people, called scribes, could read and write. Students trained for years in special schools. In time, scribes used cuneiform for much more than counting grain. They recorded laws, prayers, letters, and even long stories, such as the adventures of a king named Gilgamesh.

The achievements of Mesopotamia did not vanish when its cities fell. Ideas about writing, laws, and city life spread to other peoples and helped shape the civilizations that followed.

The passage traces a chain: irrigation, then surplus, then specialized jobs and city-states, then writing. Choice about farming being impossible contradicts the text; the others are supporting details.

Some years they came too late to help the crops, and other years they were strong enough to wash away whole villages. To control the water, farmers dug canals and built walls of earth called levees. This system of irrigation carried river water to fields that would otherwise have been too dry to farm.

Irrigation changed everything. Farmers could now grow more barley and wheat than their families needed. This extra food, called a surplus, meant that not everyone had to be a farmer. Some people became potters, weavers, metalworkers, or traders. Others became priests or leaders. As villages grew larger, they turned into city-states such as Ur and Uruk. Each city-state had its own ruler and its own temple, often a tall stepped tower called a ziggurat.

With so much trade and so many goods, people needed a way to keep track of who owned what. The Sumerians, who lived in southern Mesopotamia, solved this problem by creating one of the earliest known writing systems. At first, they pressed simple pictures into wet clay to record sheep or bags of grain. Over time, the pictures changed into wedge-shaped marks made with a cut reed. Today, this writing is called cuneiform, from a Latin word meaning "wedge."

Learning cuneiform was hard, so only a small group of people, called scribes, could read and write. Students trained for years in special schools. In time, scribes used cuneiform for much more than counting grain. They recorded laws, prayers, letters, and even long stories, such as the adventures of a king named Gilgamesh.

The achievements of Mesopotamia did not vanish when its cities fell. Ideas about writing, laws, and city life spread to other peoples and helped shape the civilizations that followed.

On a hot summer afternoon, the sky can change surprisingly fast, and a clear blue morning may turn into a dark, rumbling storm by dinnertime. To understand why, you need to know how heat and water work together in the air.

Every thunderstorm needs three ingredients: moisture, unstable air, and something to lift that air upward. Moisture usually evaporates from oceans, lakes, or damp ground. On sunny days, the sun warms the ground, and the ground warms the air just above it. Warm air is less dense than cool air, so it rises, much like a hot-air balloon. If the air higher up is much cooler, the rising air keeps going. Scientists call this condition unstable.

As the warm, moist air rises, it cools. Cool air cannot hold as much water vapor as warm air, so some of the vapor condenses into tiny droplets. Billions of these droplets form a puffy cumulus cloud. If the updraft, or rising current of air, stays strong, the cloud keeps growing taller. In a large storm, it can tower more than ten miles high, and its top may spread out in a flat shape. This giant storm cloud is called a cumulonimbus.

Inside the cloud, droplets collide and gradually grow heavier until they become too heavy for the updraft to hold up, and they fall as rain or hail. The falling rain drags cool air down with it, creating a downdraft. When people feel a sudden cold gust just before a storm arrives, they are feeling this downdraft.

Lightning forms as bits of ice crash into each other inside the cloud, building up electric charges. When the charges grow strong enough, a giant spark leaps between the cloud and the ground or between parts of the cloud. Lightning heats the air around it to about 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, which is hotter than the surface of the sun. The heated air expands so suddenly that it makes a booming sound wave. That sound is thunder.

Because light travels much faster than sound, you see lightning before you hear thunder. Weather experts offer a simple rule: if you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck. Go indoors immediately and remain there until thirty minutes after the last rumble.

The passage explains the whole process of storm formation step by step. The lightning temperature is a detail, and the other choices are not supported.

Ask a group of sixth graders to name their favorite class, and you will hear answers like art, science, or gym. You will probably not hear "cooking," because most middle schools no longer offer it. That is a mistake. Every middle school should require students to take a basic cooking class.

First, cooking teaches skills that students will use for the rest of their lives. Not everyone will grow up to solve equations for a living, but everyone needs to eat. Students who learn to make simple, healthy meals are less likely to depend on fast food when they are older. Health researchers have found that people who cook at home more often tend to eat more vegetables and less sugar than people who rarely cook.

Second, a kitchen is a hands-on classroom for other subjects. Doubling a recipe requires multiplying fractions. Baking bread shows how yeast, a living organism, produces gas that makes dough rise. At one middle school, teachers reported that students in a cooking elective became better at measuring in math class. Following a recipe also strengthens reading skills, since skipping a single direction can ruin an entire dish.

Third, cooking builds confidence and teamwork, two qualities that matter in every subject. In a kitchen, every person has a job, and the meal succeeds only if everyone does their part. My younger brother refused to eat anything green until he made his own vegetable soup at a summer cooking camp. Now he asks for broccoli.

Some people argue that schools do not have enough money or time to add another class. They point out that kitchens are expensive and that the school day is already full. These concerns are reasonable, but they can be solved. A cooking class does not need a fancy kitchen; portable burners and basic tools can cost less than a classroom set of new textbooks. Schools could also combine cooking lessons with existing science or health classes instead of adding extra hours.

Cooking is not just about food. It is about health, learning, and independence. If we want students to be ready for real life, we should hand them a whisk along with their pencils.
